News.title: Robert Bush sentence - live: Hull judge delivers verdict on horrific funeral home scandal
News.content:
Former Legacy funeral director Robert Bush gave bereaved families the wrong ashes and left bodies decomposing in what one relative described as 'the most horrendous horror story'

Former undertaker Robert Bush - who gave bereaved families the wrong ashes and left the bodies of 35 people, including a stillborn baby, decomposing - will learn his fate today.

Bush, 48, from Otley, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced for 67 offences spanning 12 years and affecting hundreds of victims at his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, in Hull. His victims included the mum of a stillborn baby boy who discovered that her child's remains had been left on a floor for two years.

It is the fifth and final day of a harrowing sentencing hearing at Hull Crown Court, during which more than 200 victims detailed the impact of Bush's crimes. They included relatives of 31 people whose bodies should have been cremated.

The court also heard Bush defrauded 226 people, taking more than £500,000 from funeral home customers after charging them for plans he was not authorised to provide.

The hearing will resume at 12pm today.

News.title: Pub owners defend chef after 'controversial' video plating roast dinner
News.content:
Pub owners defend chef after 'controversial' video plating roast dinner

The Leagate Inn in Lincolnshire shared a video of their chef plating up a pork roast dinner, but it didn't take long before the post sparked debate

View Image The owners of The Leagate Inn have hit back on social media

A pub has hit back at angry commenters following the posting of a "controversial" video featuring one of their roast dinners. The Leagate Inn in Coningsby, Lincolnshire, owned by Harry and Laura of Spaniel Inns Ltd, uploaded a Facebook clip on July 14 showing their chef plating up a pork roast dinner.

‌



The video revealed that the pub had been putting in considerable effort behind the scenes to perfect their roast dinners, proudly sharing the dish in the belief they had "nailed it". However, it wasn't long before the post turned "controversial", attracting dozens of angry remarks in the comments section.

‌



The primary bone of contention was the chef using his bare hands to arrange the food on the plate. Throughout the clip, he used his hands to position the roast potatoes, carrot, red cabbage, pork belly and Yorkshire pudding - sometimes handling items directly, and at other points guiding food that was already in tongs.

‌



The video amassed over 90 complaints about the chef's hands-on approach, with numerous viewers stating they would refuse to eat food that had been handled so extensively.

One person said: "I hate when someone has touched every piece of my food plating up. And stacking it makes the portion look tiny."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



A second added: "For goodness sakes put gloves on no one wants there dinner touched with someone else fingers all over it."

Co-owner Laura subsequently posted a video responding to the furore surrounding the "controversial" clip, offering an explanation as to why the chef had been using his hands. She said: "A couple of weeks ago, we uploaded this video to Facebook and we got so much hate from the toxic community that is Facebook. We had over 90 comments moaning about the fact that the chef was touching the food with his hands.

"EHO guidelines actually suggest against using gloves because they're not as hygienic as good hand hygiene. But anyway, it's a good job we're thick-skinned."

‌



Environmental Health Officer (EHO) guidelines confirm that disposable gloves are entirely optional when handling food, that handwashing remains strictly mandatory, and that gloves should never be used as a substitute for proper hand hygiene.

EHO inspections regularly highlight that wearing gloves can create a false sense of security, leading staff to neglect changing them or washing their hands altogether. In many cases, clean bare hands that are washed regularly prove far safer than poorly managed or overused gloves.

Support flooded in for the pub owners across social media, with chefs from around the globe rallying behind them.

Article continues below

One chef said: "I have been a chef for 10 years the only time I use gloves is handling raw meat then bin them I always wash my hands don't understand people sometimes."

A second person added: "Oh my god! What is wrong with people. Like hospitality is hard enough without all the bad negative comments! I love the pub Best Guinness so far! Keep doing what your doing the food looks amazing!".

News.title: Brits name biggest barriers to getting active - from cost to fear of judgement
News.content:
Brits name biggest barriers to getting active - from cost to fear of judgement

A poll of 2,000 adults found the cost of classes, equipment and travel puts them off moving more, alongside a lack of motivation and fear of being judged

View 4 Images Research revealed several barriers to achieving the recommended levels of exercise (Image: PinPep)

Brits have revealed the biggest obstacles to getting active, citing cost, a lack of green spaces in their local area – and the fear of being judged. A poll of 2,000 adults found that class fees (26%), equipment costs (25%) and travel expenses (19%) are putting people off moving more.

‌



A further 27% admitted to struggling with a lack of motivation, finding it difficult to maintain a consistent exercise routine.

‌



The average Brit spends 45 minutes on a typical workout session, yet 36% were unaware that the UK government recommends at least two and a half hours of moderate to intense physical activity per week. Chronic health conditions (15%) and fear of injury (15%) also ranked amongst the key barriers to getting more active.

‌



On top of this, 19% felt there simply aren't enough opportunities to get active in their local area.

The research was commissioned by KP Snacks, sponsors of The Hundred cricket tournament and the Cricket Cities fund, which aims to create opportunities for those from underserved urban communities to get active.

‌



A spokesperson for the brand said: "Something as simple as not having access to a safe green space, affordable activities or the confidence to take part can make a real difference to people's health and wellbeing.

"That's why it's so important that communities have opportunities close to home that make being active feel accessible and inclusive for everyone.

"We hope initiatives like the cricket fund can help remove some of those obstacles and inspire more people to get involved in sport and physical activity."

‌



View 4 Images Vicky Pattison picked up a cricket bat to back the launch of the KP Snacks Everyone In Fund, supporting the ECB’s Cricket Cities programme (Image: PinPep)

View 4 Images She joined local community players in East London to celebrate the new initiative (Image: PinPep)

More than half (56%) of those surveyed admitted to never having picked up a cricket bat, while 31% feel the sport simply isn't accessible in their area. However, 30% said they would be keen to give it a go - if it were available locally.

‌



Free sessions (24%), provided equipment (21%) and flexible scheduling (20%) were amongst the key factors that would encourage people to step onto the pitch.

Nearly seven in 10 (69%) of those living in urban areas said they would like to be more physically active than they currently are, compared to 62% in rural towns.

Of those who participated in the OnePoll.com study, 65% of all respondents believe greater investment should be channelled into community sport and local facilities.

‌



View 4 Images The initiative will invest £750,000 over the next three years to help break down barriers to getting active (Image: PinPep)

A spokesperson for KP Snacks added: "We know the desire to be more active is there, but for many people the opportunities simply aren't. That's why it's so important that communities have chances close to home that make being active feel accessible and inclusive for everyone.

"Everyone should have the chance to enjoy the benefits that being active can bring, regardless of where they live or their circumstances.

Article continues below

"By investing in local facilities, sessions and community programmes, we can help create environments where people feel supported to take that first step."

News.title: Suffolk fire live: Dunwich Heath blaze rages as scorched area could take 25 years to recover
News.content:
Wildlife habitats devastated by the 'utterly sickening' wildfire at Dunwich Heath could reportedly take up to 25 years to recover

A massive wildfire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk has devastated wildlife habitats which could now reportedly take up to 25 years to recover - as multiple crews continue to tackle flames.

The area along the Suffolk coast went up in flames at about 5pm on Wednesday before engulfing an area equivalent to about 140 football pitches near Sizewell B nuclear power plant . It included parts of the RSPB's Minsmere nature reserve, which is home to rare birds, including Dartford warblers, nightjars, stonechats as well as reptiles such as adders, common lizards and slow worms

Adam Rowlands, the Suffolk area manager for the RSPB, told the BBC some of the habitat "will take five, 10, 25 years to come back to what it looked like before the fire broke out".

Some 200 caravans were evacuated from the path of the blaze yesterday, with holidaymakers woken up by officials banging on their doors. At least 12 fire engines were at the scene overnight tackling smaller fires that continued to break out.

On Thursday afternoon, an EDF spokesperson said the fire was "not affecting operations at Sizewell B power station".

News.title: Manchester election results LIVE: Andy Burnham's successor as mayor to be announced in biggest ever by-election
News.content:
Reform council chief threatens to report café owner who gives free meals to hungry kids to police

A café owner who served up free meals to hungry children after food vouchers were removed has been told he will be reported to police by a Reform council leader.

Barry Ashley, who runs the Grumpy Cook in Hastings, stepped up after East Sussex County Council decided not to issue school holiday meal vouchers to struggling families over the summer. He has criticised the move, which he branded “shameless”, accusing the council of turning its back of children in poverty.

He has since been told by Andy Woolley, who heads the authority, that he will be reported to police along with Labour MP Helena Dollimore. Mr Woolley claims to have been personally attacked online and accused the pair of inciting hate and potential violence by naming him in their criticism.

The dispute follows the council's decision not to continue offering the vouchers, which are a lifeline to families. An appalled Mr Ashley responded by announcing he would offer free meals to children who need feeding at his not-for-profit cafe.

A number of local businesses have donated to help, and Mr Ashley told The Mirror he has been providing more than 70 free meals a day. Ms Dollimore has launched a petition calling for the vouchers to be reinstated, branding the council's actions "totally unacceptable" and accusing it of putting children at risk.

Mr Ashley said: "Hastings is one of the poorest towns in the country. And it is by every measure it's a deprived town. One in three of the children are living in poverty.

"And the vouchers, just to take those away without considering what they should be putting in place, without doing any risk assessment, without doing any impact assessment, it's beyond bizarre."

News.title: 'We saved £350,000 for retirement but our monthly bills are still not covered by pension'
News.content:
'We saved £350,000 for retirement but our monthly bills are still not covered by pension'

Sharon Taylor, 64, began seriously saving for her retirement 10 years ago by putting any money she got from pay rises into her workplace pension, and putting £150 a month into an investment account

View 3 Images Sharon and Sean had been saving carefully, aiming for a comfortable retirement

A couple who grafted for five decades and accumulated £350,000 in investments with the aim of enjoying retirement say their pensions don't stretch to cover their monthly outgoings.

‌



Sharon Taylor, who is now 64, said she started putting away as much as possible in a bid to seriously prepare for retirement a decade ago. She has been funnelling any additional income from salary increases into her workplace pension scheme, while also depositing £150 monthly into an investment account. She retired at 63 in March last year and by that point Sharon, from Sheffield, and her husband Sean Taylor, 61, had amassed £350,000 in investments.

‌



They thought this would be enough to sustain them until reaching state pension age at 67. Their original plan involved withdrawing £1,000 monthly from an easy access savings account, but they're now forced to take out an additional £500 each month due to spiralling living costs.

‌



Sharon and Sean's combined income from private pensions currently stands at just £1,400 per month, falling short of their £1,700 monthly expenditure. The pair now regret not putting away even more before finishing work. Fresh figures from Pensions UK reveal that a couple requires £62,700 annually to maintain a comfortable lifestyle and to retire comfortably at 60, a pension pot of £685,950 is needed.

View 3 Images Sharon and Sean

Sharon, who previously worked in customer services, said: "I never expected to have to be frugal in my retirement. Our joint monthly pension doesn't actually cover our bills.

‌



"The cost of everything has gone up; no amount of planning could predict how much the cost of living has gone up. I don't want to have to scrimp and save; we've worked our whole lives to enjoy ourselves. We thought we'd saved enough, but we haven't."

From the moment she entered the workforce aged 18, Sharon has consistently paid roughly 5% of her salary into her workplace pension scheme. A decade ago, Sharon started preparing for retirement, and whenever she received a pay rise (typically ranging from 1% to 4%), she channelled the additional income straight into her pension fund.

"I always knew I wanted to retire early," Sharon explained, noting she'll be eligible for her state pension at 67. Following the death of Sean's parents four years ago, the pair invested his entire inheritance into a stocks and shares ISA and purchased shares in high street banks, supplementing these investments with £150 monthly from their salaries when feasible.

‌



Upon Sharon's official retirement in March 2025, she merged all but two of her pension pots into a self-investment pension plan. At the point of retirement, the couple's combined net worth stood at £750,000, encompassing two properties and £350,000 in investments.

"We thought this would be ample to retire on," she explained. They allocated £5,000 of their investments into an easily accessible savings account for repairs, and £10,000 into a holiday fund, which they anticipated would cover them for two years.

Yet this year alone they've already been forced to shell out £3,000 on a replacement central heating system and £2,000 on a new front door, completely exhausting their entire budget. When Sharon hung up her work boots, she and Sean, who had retired five years prior at 55 due to ill health, had grand ambitions to spend their golden years exploring the world.

‌



However, a single fortnight's break in Italy set them back a staggering £10,000. "One holiday and the budget is gone," she said.

Sharon receives a modest £450 monthly from the two pension schemes she can tap into, while Sean draws £950 each month from his occupational pension. The pair also bring in £350 monthly by letting out a property to a relative, but with household bills and vehicle finance totalling £1,700, there's precious little remaining to see them through the rest of the month.

View 3 Images Sharon has tried to put enough aside

‌



Sharon had originally intended to take out £1,000 monthly from an instant access savings pot to cover groceries and other outgoings, but escalating prices have forced her to dip in for an additional £500 each month.

"I've worked for nearly 50 years. I never expected not to have enough," she said.

Instead of savouring their retirement years, Sharon and Sean have been forced to watch the pennies, opting for coffee and cake or a morning meal out rather than an evening dinner.

‌



"We're not going to be able to do any more holidays this year, or do other things we'd like to," she said. Sharon has contemplated returning to part-time employment to boost their income, and was last year contacted by an online travel agency.

Unfortunately, the monthly charges exceeded her earnings from the venture, prompting her to abandon the scheme. Reflecting on her past decisions, Sharon regrets not having saved more before stepping down from work.

"I wish I'd put more into my pensions, so I didn't have to stretch out what I have in the bank until the end of the month. Before you retire, really sit and think about whether you can put more into your savings.

Article continues below

"Even if it's just £5 or £10 a month. Don't make the same mistakes we made, thinking you'll have enough."

News.title: Hospice doctor 'awestruck' as dying patients all see same thing in final moments
News.content:
Hospice doctor 'awestruck' as dying patients all see same thing in final moments

A doctor who has witnessed thousands of people die has spoken a little about what he thinks happens to the brain when someone is in their final moments before death

View 3 Images A doctor has spoken about his experiences of watching people die (stock) (Image: Getty)

A doctor who has seen thousands of people die has revealed one common theme he has noticed among them.

‌



Dr Chris Kerr, a neurologist and the chief medical officer and chief executive officer of Hospice Buffalo in New York, USA, has spoken about his experiences of caring for dying patients.

‌



Dr Kerr, whose TED Talk titled ‘I see dead people: dreams and visions of the dying’ has been viewed by more than five million people, has discussed how he has seen people behave in the final moments of their lives.

‌



The researcher has been studying what are known as ELDVs (End of Life Dreams and Visions) for decades. During that time, he has recorded and analysed the experiences of patients nearing the end of their lives.

Speaking to The Times about his work, he said there was one overarching theme among those he had witnessed dying and how the ELDVs had affected them during their final moments.

He said the most common theme was that people would see visions of their family members, often deceased relatives, in dreams before they passed away.

‌



Dr Kerr told the publication: “I am awestruck by the way that patients are united with the most important people in their lives emotionally and developmentally. Often the encounters are with people they lost in childhood.”

View 3 Images There is great interest in what happens when we die (stock) (Image: Getty)

When it comes to the mechanism behind these visions, Dr Kerr said they had the added benefit of meaning people did not die alone, as they had someone with them in their final moments as they passed away — similar to being walked to a train station by a friend or family member.

‌



He said: “This means that we don’t leave this life alone but with a parent, sibling, deceased child or beloved pet.”

Dr Kerr is not the only physician to have explored what the brain is doing in its final moments, with researchers including Professor Jimo Borjigin from the University of Michigan also intrigued by what happens when we die.

Research by the university, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggested that when someone dies, their brain activity surges before the moment of death rather than simply shutting down like an electrical device being unplugged.

‌



View 3 Images Scientists are working hard to understand the dying brain (stock) (Image: Getty)

Professor Borjigin suggested there could be something known as a “cover consciousness” that does not become fully known to someone until they are close to death, and that the brain produces chemicals such as dopamine in one final burst of activity.

Using the example of cardiac arrest, she said: “The brain has an extremely sensitive mechanism to sense oxygen levels in your body. Even tiny drops of oxygen levels — the brain knows about that and constantly regulates the supply of oxygen.

Article continues below

“To think that when you are undergoing cardiac arrest — where the heart is stopping or not pumping blood — and the brain does nothing? It’s beyond me. The brain should be going crazy — which is exactly what happens.”

Speaking to the Guardian about the research, she said: “I believe what we found is only the tip of a vast iceberg. What’s still beneath the surface is a full account of how dying actually takes place. Because there’s something happening in there, in the brain, that makes no sense.”

News.title: Mysterious 'friends' Brit 'left to meet' before her body was found in suitcase in Athens
News.content:
Mysterious 'friends' Brit 'left to meet' before her body was found in suitcase in Athens

Police are trying to trace a group of mystery Americans after Brit Elisabeth-Jane Ross reportedly left pals to stay with them before her body was found inside a suitcase in Athens.

View 2 Images Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens. (Image: cretalive.gr)

A British woman whose body was found stuffed inside a suitcase in Athens had reportedly told friends she was going to spend time with a group of mystery Americans before her death.

‌



Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was discovered by a homeless man after he spotted a leg sticking out of a suitcase in a derelict building on Evelpidon Street in Athens' Kypseli neighbourhood at around 1pm on July 18.

‌



She had been staying with Greek friends in the Keratsini district, near Athens' main port, before telling them on July 15 that she was leaving to stay with Americans she knew in Kypseli, according to the Daily Mail.

‌



A police source told the Mail: "She told the Greek friends she was staying with that she was going to spend some time with American friends in Kypseli but did not provide any more details.

View 2 Images Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens. (Image: cretalive.gr)

"We have interviewed her Greek friends and there is nothing to incriminate them. They provided important information."

‌



Detectives are also investigating whether someone sent messages from Ms Ross's phone after her death in a bid to make it appear she was still alive. One message sent to a Greek friend on July 15 reportedly read: "I need some time – I'm going to a Greek island."

Her family also received messages claiming she "needed some time to herself" and "wanted to be alone for a while". Investigators believe the missing phone remained active in the Athens area until shortly before Ms Ross was formally identified, before it was switched off.

Ms Ross, born in Scotland in February 1988, is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found. She is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus last month, according to Greek public broadcaster ERT.

Article continues below

She was identified through Interpol and US databases using her fingerprints after her DNA did not match any records held in Greece, according to Greek news outlet Proto Thema. An initial forensic examination found no obvious injuries or signs of a struggle, although a post-mortem examination is expected to establish how she died.

A Police Scotland spokesperson previously said: "We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland."

A Foreign Office spokesperson added: "Our thoughts are with Elisabeth's family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities."

News.title: Senior Infantino adviser quits after Asian federation opposes World Cup investment plan
News.content:
A senior adviser to Fifa president Gianni Infantino resigned hours after a third confederation opposed his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

Carlos Cordeiro said Infantino's proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Cordeiro's resignation came after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) published a statement saying it "stands in solidarity" with its counterparts in Europe and North, Central America and the Caribbean.

The AFC added Infantino's plan could not "realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward".

"The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world's leading football nations," it said.

"Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered."

The AFC's statement means Infantino's plans are unlikely to be approved by Fifa members if put to a vote.

Infantino had indicated the proposals would need a straight majority to go through - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour for the proposal.

Uefa - the body that governs European football - has 55 votes. Concacaf, which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, has 35 and Asia has 46.

Should all member associations back the stance of their governing body, that would mean 136 nations are against Infantino's plan.

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with four offences while in prison, including assault on an emergency worker and possession of a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

Rudakubana, 19, murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a life prison sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

News.title: Satellite images show impact of heatwaves and drought on UK landscape
News.content:
Satellite imagery shows the toll taken on the UK landscape from this year's long hot summer.

BBC Verify analysis of satellite data shows where in the UK has been most affected by heatwaves and a lack of rain.

We can see parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.

Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and have an impact on agriculture and food supplies.

Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.

News.title: Anthropic's Claude AI escapes to hack into three organisations
News.content:
US technology firm Anthropic says its AI models hacked into the systems of three organisations on their own, during a private security experiment.

The models found a weakness in what was supposed to be an isolated test environment and connected to the internet.

It comes just days after rival OpenAI said that its models had breached the systems of other companies, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.

The announcement prompted Anthropic to check whether its own systems had carried out similar attacks. It says it uncovered three cases which have since been reported to the affected companies.

Anthropic, which did not name the organisations, urged other AI labs to perform similar reviews to better understand the risks of their models' capabilities.

Anthropic said in a statement, external it reviewed more than 140,000 tests to find evidence Claude - its family of AI models - had managed to get online even though it was supposed to be in an isolated test environment, cut off from the internet.

The tests included exercises in which Claude was tasked with obtaining "secret" information hidden on another machine on the closed-off network.

It was then told to get the information by breaking into the machine and finding it - a common way that experts assess a model's hacking capabilities.

A "misconfiguration" on systems run by Anthropic and its testing partner left the models with live internet access.

Treating it all as still part of the same exercise, Claude then connected to the internet and breached the systems of three real organisations rather than just test ones, the San Francisco-based firm said.

Anthropic said the earliest incidents date back to April and that it is "approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone."

Neither Anthropic nor the organisations that were breached had noticed the intrusions at the time.

Anthropic said it could have reviewed its records more thoroughly and added that the findings gave the firm "cautious optimism" that such risks can be overcome with more investment and tighter measures.

"The broader lesson is not necessarily that AI has developed a fundamentally new attack capability," cybersecurity expert David Allott from Veeam Software told the BBC.

"Instead, it is that AI agents can combine capabilities, obtain credentials and system access to take actions autonomously, while adapting scope and scale at machine speed," he added.

The incidents come as tech firms pour billions of dollars into developing AI agents that can independently perform tasks ranging from research and customer support to cybersecurity.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.

Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.

The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.

Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.

Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.

Sainsbury's bought Argos â together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â in 2016 for Â£1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around Â£720m in 2024.

In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Robert said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.

He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat products

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.

Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops â and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said areas would not need mayors to benefit from investment, because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.

She said: "We won't be imposing mayors to areas that don't want it but we will be creating strategic authorities in every area of England and they will be able to hold these powers and resources as well.

"They don't need to have mayors in order to control them or in order to retain a share of their income tax and business rates."

Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.

For example, the Lancashire strategic authority will take in Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council, Blackpool Council and Lancashire County Council, which form the Lancashire Combined County Authority area, despite the area not having a mayor.

The power to raise and control tax revenues is highly centralised in the UK, making the country an outlier by international standards.

The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, external, a global policy forum.

That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%), and the US (45.7%).

As it stands, mayors of strategic authorities in England receive most of their funding from central government grants.

During his time as Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham pushed for greater control over tax revenue, rather than having to rely on government grants.

The UK government had already been exploring whether a share of revenue from national taxes could be distributed to metro mayors, before Burnham became prime minister earlier this month.

But in a major speech on devolution in June, Burnham said he would "oversee the biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen" if he became prime minister.

Burnham has put devolution at the heart of his plan for government, arguing that metro mayors are best placed to boost economic growth across the country.

News.title: British man accused of spying on Cyprus RAF base for Iran
News.content:
A British man has been arrested on suspicion of spying on a UK military base in Cyprus on behalf of the Iranian military.

Rashad Sultanov, 44, of Islington, north London, is accused of carrying out "hostile surveillance" on RAF Akrotiri and sharing information with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

Sultanov, who also holds Azerbaijani citizenship, was arrested by Cypriot police on 17 July and is in custody pending extradition proceedings.

The Crown Prosecution Service has said he will be charged under the National Security Act - the first time an alleged offence under the 2023 law has been investigated in an overseas territory.

The UK has maintained a permanent base at Akrotiri since the 1950s and RAF operations to shoot down Iranian missiles and drones have been launched from there in recent months.

The investigation, which was led by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London, focused on alleged spying between 11 May 2025 and 22 June 2025.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of CTP London, said: "This case shows we are able to use the National Security Act overseas when British military bases are allegedly targeted by hostile state activity.

"A huge amount of partnership work has been carried out between British and Cypriot law enforcement agencies.

"We continue to work with colleagues from the CPS, National Crime Agency and Cypriot authorities as extradition proceedings progress."

News.title: What your summer reading list says about you
News.content:
You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.

But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?

"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the Ãcole Normale SupÃ©rieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality.

"When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain.

"Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."

Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.

Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.

During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:

Epic other-world adventures (action, adventure, science fiction, dystopian/post-apocalyptic, fantasy)

Everyday life and human relationships (comedy, romantic, drama, family, musical)

Threat and danger (true crime, crime/mystery/thriller, horror)

Facts and histories (documentary, biography, historical)

But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

News.title: Thames Water boss says leakage targets 'not realistic'
News.content:
Water companies have performance commitments on issues such as leakage.

It is illegal to release raw sewage into rivers and seas during "normal" weather conditions, but firms are allowed to do so when it rains heavily, to prevent homes being flooded.

Thames is the UK's largest water company, supplying water and wastewater services to 16 million customers across London and parts of southern England.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Weston said the company treats 4.3 billion litres of waste a day, and "99.5% of the time" it gets treated successfully, although "sometimes something goes wrong".

"We want to do better when it comes to pollutions," he said, but added, "the targets that the company is expected to make are not realistic.

"[For example], we have to hit a certain level of leakage, but it is so far in excess of what we are capable of doing, I think anyone would be capable of doing, however much money you invested, that it is not going to be achievable."

The chance of getting to zero pollution was "very, very slim", he added.

Ofwat told the BBC: "With around a fifth of water put into supply still lost through leakage, companies must deliver on the commitments they have been funded to achieve.

"Water company targets are intended to be ambitious and drive better outcomes for customers and the environment."

A spokesperson for the Environment Agency said: "[We] and the public expect Thames Water to comply with the law," adding that the agency would continue to hold companies to account where performance falls short.

James Wallace, chief executive of campaign group River Action, said: "Thames Water's tactics of opacity and deflection fool no-one. Telling the public to save water while this wasteful profit-obsessed corporation leaks 570 million litres of treated drinking water every day is offensive.

"There is nothing 'realistic' about accepting sewage pollution as inevitable. The choice is simple: keep propping up a failed privatised financial model, or put Thames Water into special administration and rebuild it as a public utility serving customers, rivers and the public."

News.title: BP puts North Sea business up for sale
News.content:
BP has said it is putting its North Sea business up for sale in a move that would end 60 years of production in the region by the oil giant.

The decision follows a review of BP's operations as it seeks to slim down the group. Its North Sea business has five production hubs - two in the central North Sea and three west of Shetland - and employs about 1,100 people.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.

Trump, some trade unions, industry figures and some Labour MPs all back increased drilling in the North Sea.

"The UK has been our home for more than 100 years and will continue to play an important role in our future," BP chief executive Meg O'Neill said.

"We're proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day," she said.

The company said it remained committed to operating the business safely and reliably throughout the sale process.

Its North Sea business produced 117,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2025, a small fraction of the oil giant's 2.3 million barrels of daily production.

News.title: TikToker faces police probe over secret filming using 'smart glasses'
News.content:
One of the most disturbing incidents occurs on Skye where he tells a UK-born Sikh shopkeeper of Indian heritage that there is "forced" diversity in Europe.

He goes on to refer to the Kalergi Plan - a far right conspiracy theory about a plot to "breed out the white race".

The woman, who was running the shop with help from her teenage daughter, politely suggests his comments are "slightly derogatory".

When he leaves, Margerison angrily describes her in his video commentary as "condescending" and complains that "they don't understand".

The woman, who was born in London and has lived in Skye for 20 years, told BBC Scotland News he initiated the conversation by asking "what are you doing here?" but edited this out of the published footage.

She said her encounter with Margerison, who is heavily built and well over 6ft tall, was "100% intimidating" and that she cried when she was later told by a friend that a secretly-filmed video had been published on TikTok.

"You're made to feel very small when you see a video like this," she said.

"And it's sad because everyone in the local community is really nice. This was really upsetting."

While in the Hebrides, Margerison also filmed an angry encounter with an elderly couple in a supermarket after they complained that he had "loudly and rudely" asked them to move out of his way.

He follows them around the store, at one point blocking their path, swears in front of them, accuses them of being "mental".

He also tells them he intends to post footage of them on TikTok which he says is "well within my rights".

News.title: Elderly victim of 'cruel' carer can't be left alone after being 'traumatised'
News.content:
An 81-year-old whose "cruel" carer was jailed after being caught on camera abusing her cannot be left alone because she is "traumatised," her daughter has said.

Louise Harris was given a three-month sentence after CCTV filmed her drunkenly screaming "I hope you die in your sleep... you horrible cow" at Elizabeth Anne Shipton in Pontardawe, Neath Port Talbot.

Elizabeth's daughter Tracy Faram Shipton called Harris's actions "horrific" and said her sentence for ill treatment and criminal damage was "laughable".

Despite this, the family is unable to appeal against it as, under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, external, the attorney general can only refer specific qualifying crimes to the Court of Appeal.

Harris, 42, was filmed on the family's video surveillance system, which was originally installed so Tracy and her brother could monitor their late father John in case he fell while caring for Elizabeth.

She had originally been charged with attempted robbery - a crime which would have qualified for sentencing to be appealed by the victim's family - but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) dropped that charge.

"Mum can't be left on her own at all now," Tracy added.

A CPS spokesman said: "We keep all cases under review and on this occasion concluded that our legal test was not met, as there was insufficient evidence to prosecute the defendant with attempted robbery and theft.

"We have written to the victim to explain our decision in more detail."

News.title: Famous Whale Bone Arch to be replaced by replica
News.content:
Whitby's famous Whale Bone Arch will be replaced by a bronze replica, it has been confirmed.

The clifftop structure, described as one of the town's "most recognisable and significant landmarks", is in need of replacement due to deterioration.

Real jawbones of dead whales were first raised on top of West Cliff in 1964 as a symbol of Whitby's maritime heritage. They were replaced with another genuine pair in 2002, but the new set will be more durable and less controversial.

Whitby's mayor Sandra Turner said: "Nobody wants to think a whale has been killed in this day and age, but at the same time it's Whitby's heritage. It's important we still have something up there which represents that."

North Yorkshire Council, which owns and maintains the 19ft (5.8m) tall arch, said it would be taken down in September to allow a replica of the same size to be moulded from the existing bones.

The new structure is expected to be installed early next year, according to the authority.

"Years of exposure to the weather on the coast has led to significant deterioration in the arch's condition, meaning the bones now need to be replaced," a spokesperson said.

Council executive member Mark Crane, whose responsibilities include harbours, said: "The new bronze arch will stand for generations, providing a lasting symbol of the town's unique maritime heritage and ensuring this iconic feature continues to inspire residents and visitors long into the future."

A statue of Captain Cooke, which stands just a few feet away from the current whale bones, is also made from bronze.

At an estimated Â£70,000, the bronze replica was the most expensive option put forward by the council, which will cover its cost.

"Given the feelings with people in this modern-day era perhaps it's probably the best route to go," said Turner.

"The council did try to get a genuine set of jaw bones, but there's so much legislation to bring them out of one country to another.

"The biggest problem was locating a pair of jaw bones that were of the size and condition that was suitable."

News.title: Drought conditions may worsen before improving as little rain in sight
News.content:
Conditions in the most parched areas of the United Kingdom could worsen before they improve, according to the latest forecasts.

The coming days will offer little relief to the areas that need it most, including eastern, central and southern England, and the entirety of Wales.

Meanwhile, August as a whole is showing a trend towards warmer and drier-than-average conditions.

It comes as Natural Resources Wales (NRW) extended its drought declaration to the entirety of the country on Thursday, adding that the high temperatures were causing the natural environment to "deteriorate".

It follows a similar announcement from the Environment Agency on Wednesday which plunged more than half of England into drought conditions.

News.title: MP Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension
News.content:
The long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.

In a statement, a Labour spokesperson said Abbott had "apologised" following an independent process and that she would be readmitted into the parliamentary party, meaning she can sit as a Labour MP once again.

Abbott, who was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row, said she had been "issued with a formal warning".

East Kilbride and Strathaven MP Joani Reid has also been readmitted to the party. In March, she said she had "voluntarily" suspended herself after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.

Her husband David Taylor, was arrested along with two other men. All three have been released on police bail, which in May was extended until August.

Responding to her readmittance on Thursday evening, Reid she was "excited to play a full part in supporting our new prime minister".

She added: "I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised."

News.title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
News.content:
The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.

While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement the government would "robustly defend this appeal".

Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.

The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than Â£1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.

The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year.

Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.

The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.

That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three assaults on prison staff at HMP Belmarsh.

The Metropolitan Police said that the alleged assaults occurred in 2025.

Rudakubana is serving a 52-year prison sentence for murdering Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He injured eight other children and two adults, dance class leader Leanne Lucas and businessman Jonathan Haye, in the attack.

Rudakubana was given what then-Attorney General Lord Hermer said was the “second-longest sentence imposed by the courts in English history”.

The judge in his case was unable to impose a whole-life order as the murderer was only 17 when he carried out his attack.

Thai travel YouTuber Hlun Solo has been found dead in Georgia after disappearing while travelling alone, with authorities investigating the circumstances of his death.

Hlun Solo, whose legal name was Bowornthat Pengsuk, was a 27-year-old travel content creator who had been documenting his solo trip through Georgia before his family lost contact with him on 13 July.

As days passed without any communication, relatives turned to social media to appeal for information about his whereabouts before confirming on 30 July that he had died.

Bowornthat, who documented budget backpacking trips, had built a large following in Thailand by sharing practical travel guides and solo adventures from around the world. He had visited more than 50 countries and amassed more than 770,000 subscribers before later surpassing 1 million subscribers on YouTube.

Thailand’s ministry of foreign affairs said it was coordinating with the Royal Thai Embassy in Ankara, which oversees Thailand's diplomatic and consular affairs in Georgia, and local authorities to establish the circumstances of Bowornthat's death and facilitate the return of his body.

Jaithai Upakaranitikaset, the ministry’s spokesperson and director general of its department of information, said embassy officials travelled to Georgia to meet local authorities, where they received formal confirmation of his death, according to The Nation.

open image in gallery Thai travel YouTuber Hlun Solo has been found dead in Georgia after disappearing while travelling alone ( YouTube/Hlun Solo )

Few details about Bowornthat’s death have been made public. Thai PBS World, citing Georgian media, reported that he was found dead in a hotel room in the capital Tbilisi, bringing to an end a search that lasted more than two weeks.

The broadcaster said Georgian authorities had opened an investigation under Article 115 of the country’s criminal code, which covers incitement to suicide but is routinely used when a person dies in unexplained circumstances.

Thailand’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Sihasak Phuangketkeow, said the government would wait for Georgian authorities to complete their investigation before making arrangements to return Bowornthat's remains to Thailand. “We cannot draw any conclusions at this stage. It is better to wait for the official investigation,” he told reporters at Government House in Bangkok on Thursday, adding that Georgian authorities were expected to expedite the inquiry.

Sihasak said police had accounted for the travel creator’s belongings and that officials would consult his family before deciding how and when his remains should be repatriated.

While officials await the outcome of the investigation, Bowornthat's family have appealed for the public not to speculate about how he died. His 82-year-old grandmother, Som Plengsuk, told reporters she had continued to believe her grandson would return safely, as he had after previous overseas trips, and spent days hoping for news before learning of his death.

Police action against supporters of the recent Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protests has reportedly intensified, with activists alleging nationwide crackdown on people who participated in the 36-day agitation.

A 25-year-old woman was booked for allegedly using "abusive and objectionable" language against prime minister Narendra Modi during the youth-led protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 23 July, according to the police complaint.

Local media reports quoted the police as saying that the woman from the ​Indian national capital's suburb of Noida, identified as Ruchika Singh, is absconding and is being traced.

Police in the southern Indian city of Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India’s head over Facebook posts that “depicted Mr Modi in an abusive manner”, a police official said on Friday.

Authorities are preparing to write to Meta as part of the investigation, V Aravind Babu, Hyderabad’s deputy commissioner of police for cyber crimes, said, according to Reuters.

The complaints allege that the manipulated content was derogatory, misleading, and capable of inciting public disorder.

Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment on Friday. The case ‌adds to a string of ‌tensions between Meta and Modi's government over content tied to the prime minister. India's IT ministry summoned Meta executives ⁠this week after Facebook briefly restricted Mr Modi’s post last week, with a top official saying the government wanted Meta to explain the matter at the highest level.

A Meta spokesperson said at the time that the post, which was Mr Modi's first where he addressed massive student protests that forced the resignation of the education minister, had been blocked inadvertently. Mr Modi has also come in for a ⁠barrage of online criticism, jokes and ridicule by protesters in ‌recent weeks.

Protesters have said that authorities intensified detentions in the weeks following the agitation that forced the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

One of the protest’s best-known volunteers, 24-year-old law student Mohammad Junaid, approached the Supreme Court alleging that he was illegally detained, interrogated overnight and released the following day because of his role in organising the demonstrations.

In his petition, he has also alleged that police questioned his father and searched the family’s home. Ghaziabad Police have denied the allegations relating to the search, saying only that his father was questioned, the BBC reported.

Civil liberties groups and opposition leaders have criticised the police action, while CJP leaders have accused authorities of targeting volunteers after the protests ended.

The Delhi Police has not publicly responded to Mr Junaid’s allegations.

On Thursday, Delhi Police said no legal action would be taken against people who took part in the recent protests, provided they did not have a criminal record, according to News18.

The CJP is a youth-led satirical movement whose logo is an outline of a cockroach on a mobile phone. The group's 30-year-old founder, ​Abhijeet Dipke, says CJP was so named because of comments by Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant comparing some unemployed youth to cockroaches. Kant later said ​he did not mean to criticise young people but was referring to those with “fake and bogus degrees” who were “like parasites”.

CJP spokesperson, Saurav Das, distanced the organisation from the alleged use of abusive language during the protests but criticised the use of criminal law against demonstrators.

“If any language used was derogatory in nature, then the person concerned is free to pursue civil and criminal defamation proceedings against the individual concerned. However, the use of the criminal justice machinery against protesters is highly condemnable, and no one should be punished merely for using objectionable language,” Mr Das was quoted as saying by Indian newswire Press Trust of India.

“The language may be wrong, and it may be objectionable to someone, but that is no reason to invoke the criminal justice machinery against such people. It creates a chilling effect. I don’t think this is acceptable to anybody, especially the younger generation,” he said.

“I would request the younger generation to be very careful about the words they use and the kind of insults or remarks they make against people in general,” he said.

Opposition Congress president and leader of opposition in upper house of parliament, Mallikarjun Kharge, called for the resignation of home minister Amit Shah over the police crackdown on CJP’s protests.

On Tuesday, India’s Supreme Court ordered the release of minors arrested during the protests and directed authorities to preserve CCTV footage after petitioners alleged police used excessive force against demonstrators.

Indian media reported that Mr Kant also ordered officials to preserve the digital and personal data of protesters and barred any coercive action against those who took part in the protests.

The reports said Mr Kant took interim steps in response to petitions filed by student protesters and activists seeking ​action against police and paramilitary forces for what they said was the use of excess force ⁠and pellet guns during the weeks-long demonstrations.

The government has, meanwhile, defended the police response, saying officers acted within the law to control the protests.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the Supreme Court that allegations of students being assaulted were serious, but said around 250 police personnel were also injured.

The protests, triggered by the leak of question papers for a national medical college entrance exam, ended on Saturday after the education minister resigned and the government agreed to the protesters' demands for exam reforms, withdrawal of police cases, and compensation ​for families of students who died by ​suicide after the leaks.

Indonesian authorities arrested a Malaysian pilot for allegedly smuggling at least 26kg of the synthetic drug MDMA while being on the job, the customs office said on Friday.

Officials said the pilot, identified by the initials MSO, 39, was arrested on Wednesday at the main airport of the capital city of Jakarta.

At least 14 bags of ecstasy – more than 70,000 pills – and four grams (0.14oz) of meth were found in the pilot’s suitcase, customs officials said.

The methamphetamine was found in his hand luggage and reported to be for his personal use, officials said. The pilot is believed to have flown under the influence of multiple drugs, they said.

While the airport customs office did not specify which carrier the pilot was working, the flight number suggested it was a Malaysia Airlines plane.

He flew the plane from Kuala Lumpur to Jakarta, customs officer Hengky Tomuan Palindungan Artionang.

“The results of his urine test came back positive for meth, MDMA, and cocaine. So, at the time of the flight, he was under the influence,” the official said, speaking to reporters in Jakarta.

He added: “What concerns all of us is that this person’s profession is a pilot, and at the time he arrived, he had just flown that plane from Kuala Lumpur to Indonesia.”

A urine test of the pilot right after the flight confirmed he was under the influence of cocaine and synthetic drug methamphetamine, Mr Hengky said.

The pilot is believed to have brought MDMA in a suitcase to Jakarta for an unidentified person with the promise of a reward worth around 50,000 ringgit (£9,092), the official said.

He has now been named a criminal suspect for being a courier of a drug which is covered under Indonesia’s strict drug laws.

The accused told investigators that this was the time he attempted the smuggling of banned drugs, with the previous instances being to Indonesia earlier once and to Malaysia.

If convicted, the accused can be punished to death penalty or life imprisonment under Indonesian law.

The southeast Asian nation has some of the world’s toughest anti-drug laws, including the death penalty for traffickers. However, it has abstained from executions for several years.

In 2015, an Indonesian court ordered the execution of two Australian nationals in the Bali Nine drug ring for attempting to smuggle heroin out of the resort island of Bali.

Malaysia Airlines declined to comment on the case as it was under investigation, but said it does not tolerate any form of misconduct and is currently ‌conducting an internal review into the matter.

The ​company added that it will cooperate ‌with relevant authorities.

Google DeepMind has unveiled a version of its AI model Gemini that can control humanoid robots for the first time.

The Gemini Robotics 2 system brings “intelligent whole-body control” that allows humanoids to perform a wide range of tasks autonomously.

A video demonstrating the new artificial intelligence model showed robots picking up watering cans, screwing in light bulbs and tying up bin bags.

“Most robots are pre-programmed or teleoperated for narrow, repetitive task sequences. They lack the ability to truly learn for themselves or adapt to unpredictable environments,” Carolina Parada, head of robotics at Google DeepMind, wrote in a blog post detailing the new AI model.

“For the first time, our model can now control entire humanoid robots, translating intent into intelligent whole-body control.”

Gemini Robotics 2 combines a vision language model (VLM) with two vision language action (VLA) models to allow robots to both communicate with humans and understand its environment to move around and perform tasks.

Google DeepMind described its release as a “milestone” towards achieving physical AGI (artificial general intelligence), whereby robots have human-level abilities.

“Unlocking the true potential of robotics requires moving past single task automation toward general-purpose intelligence,” Dr Parada said.

“By building this core intelligence, our goal is to enable AI in the physical world that can work alongside humans to solve complex challenges.”

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has previously outlined a vision of creating an AI system that would essentially serve as an Android operating system for robots.

By building the “brain” for humanoids, robotics companies like Boston Dynamics could focus on developing the physical hardware while relying on a common AI platform for perception, reasoning, and control – much as smartphone manufacturers build different devices on top of Android.

Last year, the company launched its first AI model for robots that allows them to operate independently without an internet connection.

The on-device system means robots can work in any location on Earth, or in space, without having to rely on far-away servers to carry out the necessary computing.

News.title: World Cup boycott latest: Infantino’s senior adviser quits after Fifa refuses to back down over Uefa protest
News.content:
Inside Uefa’s extraordinary World Cup boycott plans – and what Fifa might do next

Gianni Infantino is under mounting pressure from football federations as well as from within Fifa after Uefa’s boycott of the World Cup left his plans to privatise its tournaments in tatters.

Infantino’s long-term adviser Carlos Cordeiro, a key figure within Fifa, has quit in protest of Infantino’s proposals, while the Asian Football Confederation has become the third federation to reject them publicly, releasing a strong statement on Friday backing the stance of Uefa and Concacaf, while claiming that confidence in Fifa’s governance has been “undermined”.

It comes after Fifa hit back at Uefa, insisting that “nobody is selling football” and confirming that it will continue its consultation period ahead of a vote on 19 September. But after another federation joined Uefa’s side, Infantino looks unlikely to get the votes he needs and is instead facing growing opposition to his leadership.

On Thursday, Uefa announced that it would boycott the World Cup and all Fifa competitions if Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its major tournaments to external investors are voted through.

“Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one,” a statement said following an emergency Uefa meeting. “We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.”

The UK’s only all-women’s chess team has secured promotion to the top tier of the sport, but they have now been told they must include a man in their squad.

She Plays To Win Lionesses A Team were promoted to the first division of the Four Nations Chess League (4NCL), but a rule dictates that every squad in the competition must have at least one male player and one female.

The rule was ironically introduced to boost women’s participation in chess, but She Plays To Win may now have to sacrifice one of the team’s pieces – so to speak – by replacing a female player with a man.

The team were allowed to field an all-women’s side while competing in 4NCL’s second division, as long as one player was under the age of 18.

Per the Guardian, 19-year-old Alisha Vyas joined She Plays To Win after playing in mixed squads, often as the sole female.

“I knew I was only there to fulfil the quota as a woman, and there wasn’t that sense of community,” she said. “Being part of She Plays To Win is amazing – we have team dinners every time, and there’s real camaraderie between the girls.”

Teammate Emily Maton, 18, added that the squad was “promoted on [its] own merit” and should have to adhere to the first division’s gender rule.

“There’s no shortage of male players in the division,” said Maton. “The whole point of the team is to bring female representation when there isn’t really any at all, and they introduced this rule because there weren’t enough female players. It’s going against the entirety of the rule, and it undermines what we’re trying to do as a team.

“The expectations for me were always a lot lower than they were for male players. I’d have coaches say things like: ‘You’re very good for a girl.’ We’ve had people tell us we don’t deserve to be in this division, that we’re not good enough. We got to the top proving everyone wrong, and now this undermines that.”

Mike Truran of 4NCL said: “Since its inception in 1994, the top division has always been a mixed-team competition, each team requiring a mix of males and females.

open image in gallery Approximately 11 per cent of top-rated players are female, raising questions about the future of the sport ( Getty/iStock )

“We remain the only league in the UK, that we are aware of, that encourages female participation in chess by requiring mixed teams.

“We surveyed all the team captains during the 2025/2026 season about whether the rule should be changed; there was no significant appetite on the part of the captains to do so. We remain open to changing the rule in future should captains’ opinions change.

“There is no evidence that the rule as it stands discourages female participation in chess. Indeed, we believe that – by requiring all teams in the top division to have at least one female player – we actively encourage female participation in chess.

“We believe that changing the rule to one that has no mixed-team requirement at all, such that teams in the top division are not required to include a female player, would serve to actively discourage female participation in chess.”

News.title: Senior dating: a guide to finding love later in life
News.content:
Whether you’re a widow, widower or divorcee, the thought of online dating in later life can feel daunting. However, more and more people are turning to the internet to find romance. Roughly 16 per cent of UK adults are using online dating services to meet a partner, according to Statista. Among them, there are lots of singles over 50 using dating sites.

So here’s how to navigate your senior dating online, with expert advice from psychologist and dating coach Dr Pam Spurr, and sex and relationship coach Angela Vossen.

How do I know if I'm ready to date again as a senior?

Coming out of any relationship is hard. If you’re hoping to date after a divorce, bereavement or break up, it can take a long time to feel ready to date again. Dr Spurr advises taking your time.

“Many people feel bruised, even traumatised, after coming out of a long-term relationship or having been bereaved,” she explains. “Your feelings naturally vary from day to day about whether you're ready to get back out to look for love – or even for fun. A crucial factor is if you've come to the point where you have more good days compared to bad days”.

Dr Spurr explains that good days are the days on which you feel more optimistic about life generally, and you find your thoughts turning to meeting someone new. “That's an important sign that you are healing,” she says. “However, if you're still feeling deeply insecure or are riddled with self-doubt about your worthiness, take your time. When you feel worthy, you will find someone worthy of you”.

Feeling heartbroken? Learn how to get over a break up

How to start senior dating online

If you’re new to online dating, it can feel intimidating at first. The secret is taking things step by step so that you do things at your own pace. The first step, however, should be choosing a senior dating site that will help match you with like-minded people. This will narrow your search and ensure your dating experience is more successful.

Step 1: Create an online profile

Once you’ve decided on a dating site or app and signed up, you’ll be asked to write a dating profile. This should reflect who you are along with your passions, values and what you seek in a partner.

Try to be authentic rather than creating a fantasy version of yourself. If you exaggerate your accomplishments, your date will only feel deceived once they get to know you. Likewise, don’t be tempted to use a photo of yourself from 10 years ago.

What are you waiting for? |  Single and looking to find true love? Sign up today for Telegraph Dating and join more than 220,000 like-minded people. Join today

Step 2: Spark meaningful chats with potential dates

Once you have signed up to a senior dating site and created a profile, you will be free to start looking at other people’s profiles and sending messages to anyone that catches your attention. But how can you initiate a conversation after an introduction?

“When messaging people on dating sites, ask open-ended questions to spark meaningful chats,” says Angela. A good example would be, ‘I can see you enjoy travel. What place have you always wanted to visit but haven’t yet?’ or “tell me more about your love of tennis? Did you watch the US Open?” If things go really well and the chat seems to flow naturally, you may decide to organise a phone chat or ask them out on a date. An initial chat over the phone can help gauge how well you get on and how easily the conversation flows. If this goes well, meeting in person may feel less nerve wracking and a little less ‘blind’.

Step 3: Prioritise your safety

“While most people are well intentioned online, it’s important to protect your safety,” advises Ms Vossen. “Keep personal details private (like where you live or your social media profiles) until you’ve met in person and built trust”. You should also arrange first dates in public places, share your plans with a friend, and trust your instincts if something feels off.

If the first date or two doesn’t quite hit the mark, try not to be too disappointed and remember that you can say no to another date. Ms Vossen says: “Be patient – online dating takes time, but with practice, you’ll gain confidence and enjoy the journey”.

Traditional ways to meet senior singles

Of course, couples continue to meet in a manner that predates online dating sites. If you’re keen to join the older dating scene but find the online world overwhelming, there are plenty of ways to meet people in real life.

1. Holidays and group trips

We are often our best selves on holiday, so it’s the ideal place to find a single senior woman or to meet men if the opportunity presents itself. Why not organise a trip on which you meet new people while doing what you love, whether that’s cycling, walking, sightseeing or just travelling around a new part of the world. There are many escorted tours that cater to specific age groups and interests. They also take away the stress of organising a trip yourself.

“An organised holiday or trip can be a great place to meet someone new and there are many organisations offering these for the over 50s,” says Dr Spur. “A word of caution though, you can spend a lot of money and there's no guarantee that you will meet that special person. However, if it's a place you've wanted to travel to then go with the mindset that you're going to have a great trip. If you meet someone, that's an added bonus”.

2. Activities and social groups

Whether you enjoy walking, reading or volunteering, taking up a new hobby or joining a social group is a great way to enhance your social life and increase your chances of meeting a new romantic interest.

“Joining a club or taking up a hobby can be a fantastic way of meeting singles who enjoy the same pastimes,” says Dr Spur. “You're doing an activity you enjoy knowing that there might also be someone there that will catch your eye”.

If you do meet someone that you’re interested in at a social event, Dr Spur advises starting with a simple ‘hello’ and an easy question such as how long they've been doing that particular activity or hobby. “This can open-up a friendly conversation that might lead to flirting down the line,” she says.

Start online dating for seniors today

Whichever way you decide to start looking for love, approach it in a way that you feel comfortable with. Signing up to an online dating service is a great way to meet other seniors. Remember, it’s never too late to begin a new chapter.
