Sports.title: Fifa to push ahead with consultation plan despite backlash and insists ‘nobody is selling football’
Sports.content:
Fifa is facing calls for an urgent review of its governance after insisting that the planned World Cup sell-off will continue despite the threat of a boycott from all 55 European nations.

In a strongly worded statement issued on Friday morning the Asian Football Confederation backed Uefa and Concacaf’s opposition to the creation of a new commercial company, Fifa Forward Enterprise, saying it “cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward”, and urging Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”.

Fifa had attempted to double down on its position overnight, releasing a statement at 4am UK time saying “we will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA [member association] has the ability to express its vote based on facts,” but it is now clear Gianni Infantino is facing united opposition to his proposals from around the globe.

Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC constitute 143 of Fifa’s 211 members so if their coalition remains united there is no prospect of Infantino getting the votes he needs.

The 56-year-old’s position as Fifa president is also under threat for the first time since he was elected in 2016, unless he backs down quickly.

While stopping short of matching Uefa’s boycott the AFC went further than Concacaf in clearly stating that the FFE proposal should be dropped.

“The AFC stands in solidarity with Uefa and Concacaf in expressing serious concerns over Fifa’s proposal to introduce private investment into Fifa’s flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE,” its statement read. “The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game.

“Football should never have been placed in such a position. Against this backdrop, and in light of the clear positions expressed by Uefa and Concacaf as well as the unprecedented divisions that have emerged across the football world, the AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.

“The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world’s leading football nations. Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered.”

The AFC echoed Uefa and Concacaf’s complaints about a lack of consultation from Fifa, making clear that it is not the first time confederations and the Fifa Council have been excluded from major decisions, most notably hosting arrangements for the 2030 and 2034 World Cups.

View image in fullscreen Fifa president Gianni Infantino stands with US president Donald Trump after this year’s World Cup final. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

“The AFC sees this moment as a catalyst for strengthening institutional practices,” the statement continued. “While every Fifa MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote.

“It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“The AFC calls upon Fifa to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by Fifa’s statutory bodies.”

Fifa had attempted to blame media reporting for the widespread opposition to its scheme, but it is now clear that will not wash with most of its member associations.

“We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation,” a Fifa statement read. “Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports.

“We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA [member association] has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

“FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all Fifa member associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself.

“Nobody is selling football. This is not something Fifa would ever entertain. Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world. Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of Fifa.”

If Fifa refuse to back down the first step of the threatened European boycott will come at next month’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup, with senior Women’s World Cup qualifiers to follow in October.

Sports.title: Franco Baresi, Milan and Italy legend, dies aged 66
Sports.content:
The former Milan and Italy defender Franco Baresi, one of the most recognisable players of the ⁠golden era of Italian football in the 1980s and 1990s, has died at the age of 66.

“The entire history of ⁠AC Milan is in ⁠tears following the ​passing of Franco Baresi,” his former club said on Friday. “His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club’s DNA, just as his iconic No 6 shirt is.”

Last year Baresi’s former club, where he served as honorary vice-president, said he had undergone surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule, and had ⁠been prescribed recovery treatment by a cancer specialist.

In February, Baresi was one of the torchbearers for the Olympic ​flame at the opening ceremony for the Milano ‌Cortina Winter Games, appearing alongside ‌former Inter and Italy defender Giuseppe Bergomi, his longtime rival on the pitch.

Baresi is regarded as a Milan icon, having spent his entire 20-year career with the club, winning six Serie A titles and three top European trophies, and captaining the team for 15 seasons before retiring in 1997.

At the end of his playing career, Milan retired his No 6 shirt, making him the first player in the club’s history to receive that honour.

View image in fullscreen Baresi and Juventus captain Gianluca Vialli in 1992 in Turin. Photograph: Etsuo Hara/Getty Images

Baresi was part of the Italy squad that won the ‌1982 World Cup and captained the team to the 1994 final, which ended in a narrow penalty shootout loss to Brazil, with Baresi among the players who failed to ​score. He famously played the full 120 minutes just 25 days after knee surgery.

His loyalty to Milan was established early in his career, as he stayed with the club through two relegations to Serie B in the early 1980s and helped guide them back to the top flight on both occasions.

Baresi was the cornerstone of the Milan and ⁠Italy defences for nearly two decades, captaining the Serie A club during the most ​successful period in their history and ​earning 81 caps for the national ​team.

View image in fullscreen Franco Baresi playing for Italy against Malta during a World Cup qualifier in December 1992. Photograph: Colorsport/Rex

In an era dominated by physical defenders, Baresi distinguished himself through his reading of ​the game, redefining the ‌sweeper role by combining ​defensive authority with the ​ability to launch attacks from deep.

He marshalled a celebrated Milan backline featuring Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta and Mauro Tassotti, helping perfect the high defensive line and offside trap that underpinned the club’s 58-match unbeaten run in Serie A and earned Fabio Capello’s side the nickname “Gli Invincibili” (the Invincibles).

Sports.title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches
Sports.content:
The FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.

The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.

Across the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.

Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.

“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.

Sports.title: Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubs
Sports.content:
The Premier League has agreed on a proposal to reset financial distribution within English football’s top four divisions, one that would lead to an extra £1.5bn being shared across the pyramid over the next decade.

Clubs voted unanimously to support the so-called “new deal for football” at a meeting on Thursday, after discussions with the EFL. The offer will now be presented to the EFL’s board for consideration.

According to details originally published by Sky News, the Premier League’s offer would run for 10 years and result in an additional £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs on top of the £1.6bn currently distributed to clubs and communities every three years. Some of the money would be put into discrete funds – a “lifeboat” fund for clubs in immediate crisis and one that is directed exclusively at infrastructure.

To cover the extra costs, Premier League clubs have reportedly agreed to raise the transfer levy applied to all top-flight deals from 4% to 6%. The Guardian reported this week that Manchester City were initially opposed to increasing the levy.

The Premier League said in a statement that its clubs had “unanimously voted to approve a funded proposal for a new strategic partnership with the EFL”. It said it would now “look forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal” and remain “committed to finding a football-led solution”.

The EFL has yet to officially receive the offer but acknowledged “constructive” discussions with the Premier League and said its board would “review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League”.

This is the first time that Premier League clubs have officially agreed a proposal that could be put to the EFL since they were first asked to give more money to the rest of the pyramid five years ago. The Covid pandemic had revealed the precarious nature of finances at many EFL clubs and in 2022 the then sports minister Nigel Huddleston said the British public were already “out of patience” over a failure to reach an improved settlement.

The belief that the Premier League’s riches could be shared more effectively across the game helped lead in part to the creation of the Independent Football Regulator, which came into being last year. The regulator has played no direct part in the negotiations, but has a “backstop” power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

While there is cautious optimism that a deal can now finally be agreed, it is not a guarantee that the EFL will accept the Premier League’s offer, with sources suggesting it sees the proposal as being very similar to one that was mooted in 2023 but ultimately never approved by Premier League clubs. Both sides say they remain committed to ongoing dialogue.

Sports.title: Jaissle heads for Newcastle after success in Saudi Arabia that has eluded so many
Sports.content:
Taking over a big, underachieving port city club with a loyal fanbase that is desperate for success should not faze Matthias Jaissle. Should he take the role vacated by Eddie Howe, the 38-year-old German will leave Jeddah as a hero and arrive in the north-east as one of the most successful coaches in the history of Asian football.

A decade younger than Howe, Jaissle has achieved plenty, not only surviving in a Saudi Pro League that chews through coaches at a rapid rate but emerging victorious. It also helps that Al-Ahli and Newcastle share the same Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) owners.

Newcastle fans may know little about the former centre-back, whose playing career was cut short by injury, but that was also the case in Saudi Arabia when he arrived three years ago. Austria’s Bundesliga is not followed much in Asia, so two titles won with Red Bull Salzburg did not mean a great deal: neither did Jaissle’s association with Ralf Rangnick.

Fans were more focused on Al-Ahli’s recent return to the top flight, after a first season in the second tier, and were contemplating an influx of big-name players. A little different to the situation at St James’ Park with stars such as Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon already gone and others seemingly about to follow.

In Jeddah, Riyad Mahrez, Roberto Firmino, Édouard Mendy, Franck Kessié and others arrived in a summer when the club was acquired by PIF. For a team that had been in the doldrums a year earlier, it was quite a turnaround.

Despite all that Al-Ahli may have been the perfect club for Jaissle. The fans are famously passionate but had only one domestic league win since 1984. In Asia there had been two comprehensive Champions League final defeats. Compared to Al-Hilal, Al-Nassr and Al-Ittihad – also in the PIF stable – the Green corner of Jeddah had been relatively starved of success and, for a while, challenging again was enough.

For the then 35-year-old, dealing with such names did not seem a problem. His straight-talking style, with the foreign stars treated the same as the locals, drew a positive response. With his wealth of attacking talent Jaissle tried to win possession as high as possible to give players such as Mahrez the chance to shine. His preferred attack-minded, high-intensity playing style may move up a gear by the North Sea compared to the heat and humidity of the Red Sea.

View image in fullscreen Galeno (right) was a key signing for Al-Ahli under Jaissle and brought the best out of Ivan Toney in attack. Photograph: Reuters

In his first season Al-Ahli finished third, 11 points ahead of their fierce local rivals Al-Ittihad and, crucially, qualified for the AFC Champions League Elite. The second season was more difficult, for a while at least. After the departure of Allan Saint-Maximin, Jaissle wanted a replacement winger but, instead, Ivan Toney was signed and the England striker started slowly. Results dipped but were improving by January 2025 when the axe threatened to fall. Max Allegri was ready to take over, the kind of eye-catching coach that fans often want. But not in this case – members of the Green Army supported Jaissle, who had always taken time out to praise and talk to fans. A group of them appeared at the training ground with banners telling club management they should be the ones to go.

And it worked. Al-Ahli said Jaissle was staying with their full support. In came a winger, Galeno from Porto, and with the Brazilian getting the best out of Toney, Al-Ahli moved up a gear. They finished fifth in Jaissle’s second season but got more points. It was all about the Champions League, however. In the semi-finals, they defeated Al-Hilal, 19-time Saudi and four-time Asian winners. Then, in May 2025, in front of 60,000 fans in Jeddah, Kawasaki Frontale of Japan were defeated.

Then Al-Ahli did it again, winning the Asian title for a second time last May to become the first team since their Jeddah rivals, Al-Ittihad (in 2004 and 2005), to clinch successive Champions League crowns.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They also had a title challenge at home that only faded in the final weeks with Toney scoring 32 goals. In 34 games the team collected 81 points, 14 more than the previous season, and had Al-Nassr and Al-Hilal not been so consistent then it could have been a spectacular double.

The focus for the new season, due to start in August, was all about the Saudi Pro League title; but that should be someone else’s concern now.

Jaissle was recently linked with Al-Hilal and while that wouldn’t have gone down well with fans in Jeddah, he heads to Newcastle with the blessing of most. The German was always likely to return to Europe, and departs with success in Saudi Arabia, having won major titles. Many more experienced coaches have failed in that regard. Newcastle will be a different and tougher challenge.

He is not part of the elite any more but taking Newcastle closer to the Premier League’s top four would be a good start.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Guimarães set for Arsenal? Newcastle to bring in Froholdt?
Sports.content:
Eddie Howe presumably won’t be reading this page for a while. Perhaps the now departed Newcastle boss will be seeking some beach time, looking out to sea and mentally preparing his audition for the England job while his assistant Jason Tindall works on trying to be as quick over the first few yards as Anthony Barry.

The Magpies fly out to La Manga on Friday for a pre-season training camp and it remains to be seen if Bruno Guimarães, a £75m Arsenal target, will turn up to the airport, meet them in Spain or send the lads a farewell on social media while house-hunting in London. Very latest reports suggest a deal to the champions has “moved closer” following Howe’s exit.

So what about the rest of the dwindling Magpies squad? Left-back Lewis Hall is being linked with Manchester United following the upheaveal at St James’ Park which has seen Howe depart in the wake of losing Sandro Tonali to Spurs and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona. And there are further reports suggesting the Brazil midfielder, Joelinton, may have the hump too and is seeking a move to Saudi Arabia.

Which brings us to the man seemingly set with the task of sorting out all this Tyneside turmoil. Matthias Jaissle, a 38-year-old German man, has been a big hit with Al-Ahli – handily, Newcastle share the same Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) owners – so the chatter has already started about the club’s likely new boss raiding his old team and bringing Ivan Toney back to the Premier League.

More realistic targets lie elsewhere and, with the exit of Guimarães in mind, Newcastle have a close eye on FC Porto star Victor Froholdt. They reportedly watched the Danish midfielder several times last season and would expect to pay around £70m for the 20-year-old, who already has 12 caps for his country. Eintracht Frankfurt’s Hugo Larsson and former Nottingham Forest man, Danilo, now at Botafogo, are also being linked.

While Liverpool’s players argue among themselves about who should have the captain’s armband when Virgil isn’t about, the Reds could urgently do with beefing up the squad as the summer window drifts into August. With holes in central defence and right-back, the ideal solution would be a player who could operate in both positions – an injury-free Joe Gomez basically. Step forward Bournemouth’s James Hill, a player Liverpool boss, Andoni Iraola, knows well of course. It could cost the Reds £40m to reacquaint the pair.

Curtis Jones, a prominent figure in armband-gate, continues to be linked with Inter while transfer clue-hunters were sent into a right old tizzy when Dominik Szoboszlai said “if he comes back” when referring to fellow midfielder Alexis Mac Allister during a post-match interview about Liverpool’s leadership group. Mac Allister has been linked with Real Madrid.

In terms of perfect fit, it surely doesn’t get any better than Cristian Romero to Atlético Madrid and it’s understood that the Spaniards have rekindled their interest in the Spurs centre-back.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And in ‘Do one’ news, Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso wants four or five central defenders moved on from his bloated squad, with the club looking to sell Benoît Badiashile, Trevoh Chalobah and Axel Disasi for a combined fee of around £90m.

Sports.title: Maxence Lacroix joins ‘beautiful club’ Chelsea as John Stones seals Inter deal
Sports.content:
Maxence Lacroix has joined Chelsea from Crystal Palace to become the club’s fifth signing of the summer. The France international, who won the FA Cup and Conference League with Palace, was the Blues’ main defensive target of the window.

Lacroix, 26, signs a six-year deal with Xabi Alonso’s side. “I am really happy to be part of this beautiful club,” said Lacroix, who played three times for France at the World Cup, including in their 6-4 bronze medal match defeat by England.

“Everyone knows the legend of Chelsea, its tradition of winning, and to be a part of that is a proud moment. I think it’s the best move for me because it’s the best club in the world. When I spoke with the manager, I saw that we have the same direction and desire for this club.

“We want to win. When you see the quality of the players here, everything we have around the club, it’s something that we can achieve. The ambition is to lift trophies, and I can’t wait to contribute.”

Chelsea had been looking to add experience to their back line having missed out on Rennes’ Jérémy Jacquet in January, with the player opting to join Liverpool. Levi Colwill, who is considered to be a key part of the club’s long-term plans, missed almost all of last season with an anterior cruciate ligament injury, with Wesley Fofana and Trevoh Chalobah forming the central-defensive partnership for much of the campaign.

After a dismal season that saw the club finish 10th, the club’s hierarchy has acknowledged a change in recruitment policy is needed, with a refocusing away from young, inexperienced players towards ones that can help the team compete for the title.

Lacroix, who made 55 appearances last season for Palace, has been one of the league’s most consistent defenders since moving to Selhurst Park from Wolfsburg in 2024.

The Blues confirmed the club-record arrival of Aston Villa forward Morgan Rogers last week, and have also added Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, striker Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and Sporting Lisbon’s Geovany Quenda.

Chelsea also look set to sign Brighton’s Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson after his contract with Brentford was terminated.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

John Stones has joined Inter on a two-year contract, the Serie A club have announced.

The England centre-back was a free agent after leaving Manchester City and had attracted interest from clubs across Europe.

The 32-year-old ended his 10-year stay at City in June. He made 295 appearances for the club after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016 and won six Premier League titles, three FA Cups and a Champions League title.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership returns with McInnes adding new twist to Old Firm rivalry
Sports.content:
Only residents of cloud cuckoo land can hold the firm belief that Scottish football will emerge promptly from a summer of discontent. The onset of a new domestic season, ordinarily a cause for excitement, instead gives reason to ponder the grim realities of what came before.

That it is unsurprising there has been no detailed explanation or plan from the Scottish Football Association following a lamentable World Cup does not prevent the scenario from being so deflating.

Mike Mulraney, the president, was last seen peeking out from the crowd behind Gianni Infantino and the US president at Trump Tower. Ian Maxwell, the Scottish FA’s chief executive, bemoaned “hysterical commentary” around his country’s World Cup performance during a brief media appearance after Steve Clarke had resigned. These executives had all but spurted with laughter when it was suggested handing Clarke a four-year contract immediately before Scotland set sail for the United States was perhaps a needless dalliance with risk.

Perhaps Mulraney and Maxwell are too engrossed in the sourcing of Clarke’s replacement to speak out on the overall state of the national sport. It is only fair to give them the opportunity to appoint a coach who can oversee much-needed transition in a geriatric Scotland squad.

The nation’s leading clubs have been moot on a big picture they wilfully ignore but that was exposed at a World Cup. The problem is that lingering and legitimate anger over Scotland’s showing on the biggest stage – despite all rationale behind it – mirrors so much broader sentiment as the Premiership returns. This has scope to be a troublesome, toxic campaign.

Celtic’s supporters remain irate at the custodians of their club, whom they perceive as complacent and out of touch. In Derek McInnes, Rangers have a new manager who is deeply unpopular on the other side of the city. Nobody should underestimate the lingering resentment that exists among followers of Hearts over the way the campaign of 2025-26 concluded.

The most reprehensible element of that arrived on 11 June, when the Scottish Professional Football League published the outcome of a disciplinary process into the pitch invasion that forced the ending of Celtic’s title-clinching clash against the Edinburgh club.

View image in fullscreen Celtic fans run on to the pitch after their team went 3-1 up against Hearts in the title-deciding game. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Snuggled in alongside wrist tickles for Hamilton Academical, Inverness and Stenhousemuir was a meagre fine for Celtic and a suspended, paltry ticket reduction. Rangers fans, who need little encouragement to rail against officialdom, were subdued until McInnes was slapped with a touchline ban for comments made against a refereeing decision.

Rangers have criticised elements of an independent report into the chaos which followed their March Scottish Cup loss to Celtic. Motherwell are speaking with lawyers due to objection to a Scottish FA fine for a video posted on social media.

A 2-0 European qualifying first-leg defeat in Kosovo last week was rightly sufficient to send Hibs fanatics into the internet’s version of orbit. Such results stopped being a shock long ago.

Certain clubs do actually have reasons to be cheerful. Celtic’s signing of Kasper Høgh for a club record fee not only demonstrated the kind of fiscal muscle-flexing that supporters wish happened more often but provided the most intriguing transfer arrival of the close season. Scepticism exists over the ability of players to perform outside the perennially successful environment of Bodø/Glimt.

Without such doubts and at a fee which even many Championship clubs would think little of, Høgh would have moved long ago. The 25-year-old, though, has a physical profile and direct style that should succeed in Scotland.

Celtic’s challenge is to replace existing first-team performers – Arne Engels and Alistair Johnston the prime examples – should irresistible bids arrive without posting the kind of net profit that makes balance sheets look more important than trophies. Fans have rightly welcomed the Høgh signing but need more.

Rangers, in contrast to their oldest foes, have burned through extraordinary amounts of cash in recent years while generally watching others lift trophies. This has fuelled rage in and reputational damage from the stands, which an American ownership has curiously opted not to challenge.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In McInnes, Rangers – who kick off the season at Dundee United on Friday – have a manager whose knowledge of club and culture looks better placed than most before him in recent years to lay gloves on Celtic. Vanja Dragojevic looks a smart midfield signing from Partizan Belgrade. Rangers need attacking spark yet it should be no surprise that McInnes’s first act was to implement a stronger core. He lacks nothing in motivation or work ethic in the job he has always craved. This version of Rangers should be much improved. Yet on the simple basis of course and distance specialism, Celtic remain the title favourites.

View image in fullscreen Motherwell’s recent success offers a template for other top-flight clubs to follow. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Nobody linked to Hearts should have been expected by now to fully process the circumstances in which they came within minutes of a first title win in 66 years, only for that dream to be snatched away. McInnes’s departure for Rangers, the completely new style implemented by Wouter Vrancken and a palpable raising of expectations all contribute to a period of upheaval.

Hearts’ tilt at glory came earlier than anyone could anticipate. The club remains on the minds of people who previously had no interest in the Scottish game. A comprehensive Champions League qualifying defeat by Sturm Graz showed the scale of work Vrancken has ahead of him. Patience, however, would be wise.

Motherwell’s work with and post the management of Jens Berthel Askou proved those below the Premiership’s biggest fish needn’t only cling on for dear life. The football was superb, the attendance figures boosted and a broader market was impressed. Motherwell’s sales of Elijah Just and Elliot Watt for multimillion pound fees completely justify a club model that thinks outside the box.

St Mirren have clear aspirations of introducing more young players and a more alluring brand of football. Kilmarnock displayed that at the end of last season under Neil McCann. Aberdeen will surely be a stronger force this time under Stephen Robinson.

Only one artificial pitch remains in Scotland’s top flight, which provides cause for celebration.

Football remains a Scottish obsession. It is also undeniably a sick patient. The dawning of a fresh season should appeal only if there is a glimpse of fresh thinking.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer reveals stance on trademarked celebration after Morgan Rogers joins Chelsea
Sports.content:
Cole Palmer has warned Morgan Rogers he'll send the bailiffs round if he does his trademarked 'cold' celebration.

Rogers joined Chelsea for a club-record £117million earlier this month, reuniting with Palmer.

2 Palmer trademarked the 'cold' celebration last year Credit: Chelsea FC via Getty

The pair were on the books at Manchester City before Rogers moved to Middlesbrough in 2023 following a succession of loan spells.

That same summer, Palmer joined Chelsea, and became an immediate hit in west London having scored 22 times and provided 11 assists in his debut Premier League campaign.

It meant Palmer regularly broke out the 'cold' celebration, which Rogers also performs when he scores.

Palmer trademarked the celebration with the UK Intellectual Property Office last year, even if his new Chelsea teammate was the first to do it in a professional game.

As Rogers was on international duty with England for the 2026 World Cup, the former Aston Villa man is yet to link up with the Blues squad.

Even so, the English attacking pair have been messaging frequently over the summer once it became clear Rogers would pass up the chance to sign for Arsenal in favour of Chelsea.

During Chelsea's pre-season tour of Australia, Palmer was asked about a potential celebration clash.

"We’ve never spoke about it," Palmer replied. "It’s one of them. He does it. I do it.

"I’ve trademarked it so if he tries to do anything, he’ll have the bailiffs at his door.

"Nah, we’ll do it together."

2 Rogers actually performed the 'cold' celebration in a professional match before Palmer Credit: AFP

Chelsea Pensioners

The Blues have enjoyed an active summer having followed up the additions of Marcos Palestra and Rogers with the addition of Maxence Lacroix on Thursday.

And having previously prioritised youth, Chelsea have switched focus to experience.

Xabi Alonso's side are on the cusp of signing 35-year-old striker Danny Welbeck from Brighton.

Welbeck will be joined at Stamford Bridge by compatriot Jordan Henderson after he terminated his Brentford contract.

The 36-year-old is now free to join Chelsea, and is expected to complete his switch across the capital imminently.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes asks Newcastle to delay pre-season travel plans to finalise Arsenal move
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimaraes has asked Newcastle United to delay his travel to La Manga for a pre-season training camp as he closes in on a move to Arsenal.

Newcastle insist Guimaraes was always due to join up with the party on Sunday, but sources close to the player have told talkSPORT his original travel plans moved.



2 Guimaraes has been heavily linked with a Newcastle exit this summer Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

There is no suggestion Guimaraes is refusing to travel or train, but the small delay could allow a transfer to be finalised.

Newcastle insist Guimaraes return was always a fluid situation off the back of the World Cup and that his first training day in La Manga was Monday, which remains the case as it stands.

The revelation comes days after news emerged that Arsenal were confident they could strike a deal for the Brazil international.



Arsenal believe they have a verbal agreement north of £75million in place to sign the 28-year-old.

The Premier League champions have already agreed personal terms with the Newcastle captain, talkSPORT understands.



It comes one day after Eddie Howe's surprise exit, with incoming boss Matthias Jaissle set to inherit a depleted squad.

Star players Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon have already left for big transfer fees this summer.



Newcastle are under no pressure to sell Guimaraes, who still has two years left to run on his current deal at St. James' Park.

However, the Brazilian's departure would be a huge blow for the Magpies.

2 Guimaraes' exit would be a huge blow for a depleted Newcastle squad Credit: Getty

Guimaraes has been a first-team regular for Newcastle since his January 2022 arrival from French side Lyon.



Who have Newcastle signed this summer?

Newcastle have brought in new faces to ease the exit of Tonali and possible departure of Guimaraes.

Teenage Dutch midfielder Sean Steur swapped Ajax for St. James' Park earlier this month.

And the 18-year-old has been joined at Newcastle by Aladji Bamba, who signed from French side Monaco.

Newcastle have also brought in winger Bazoumana Toure and goalkeeper Ewen Jaouen from Hoffenheim and Reims, respectively.

Sports.title: What is Cole Palmer’s goal celebration? Origins of Chelsea star’s ‘cold’ pose are from bond with new teammate Morgan Rogers
Sports.content:
What is Cole Palmer’s goal celebration? Origins of Chelsea star’s ‘cold’ pose are from bond with new teammate Morgan Rogers

Cole Palmer struggled last season, but he will hope to be whipping out his trademarked celebration much more this term.

The 24-year-old still managed to score 10 Premier League goals in 2025/26 though, using his 'cold' gesture a few times.



3 Palmer's 'cold' celebration is now trademarked by him Credit: Getty

His form since moving to Chelsea from Manchester City in 2023 has helped generate an army of fans with his custom move.

The signature celebration has gone global, appearing in the NBA and being replicated by many other sporting stars.

In fact, it's so famous that Palmer has actually officially trademarked the celebration, along with the name 'Cold Palmer' and his autograph in October 2025.



The Englishman is synonymous with the 'shiver' or 'cold' pose after scoring, seeing him rub his arms as if feeling the winter weather.

But did he actually create the celebration himself?

Where does Palmer’s goal celebration come from?

Palmer first did his 'cold' gesture after scoring two goals in Chelsea's 3-2 win over Luton Town in December 2023.



His former teammate Noni Madueke told TNT Sports after the match: "That's why they call him 'Cold Palmer', innit?"

However, Palmer himself revealed that it was actually a nod to his now-Blues teammate Morgan Rogers.



Rogers, who has joined his friend at Stamford Bridge this summer from Aston Villa, was at the time playing for Middlesbrough and had done the celebration after scoring against West Bromwich Albion.

Palmer admitted: "My boy Morgs did one for Middlesbrough, so I told him I’d do it too if I scored."

3 Rogers actually performed the 'cold' celebration in a professional match before Palmer Credit: AFP

But he then continued his electric goalscoring form in 2024 and soon the celebration became synonymous with him.



Rogers went on to join his close friend in the Premier League after arriving at Villa the following month and the pair shared a pitch when Unai Emery's side drew 2-2 with the Blues in April.

He scored his side's second goal of the game against Chelsea and was accused of copying Palmer when he did the 'cold' pose.

However, discussing the moment afterwards, Rogers insisted: "He definitely copied me. It’s my celebration. Check the timeline, I did it first."

In response, Palmer spoke to talkSPORT in 2024 about who the real owner of the celebration was, saying: "We've [him and Rogers] had a chat about this. He knows I did it and it took off.



"Everyone knows it's my celebration. He [Rogers] might have done it, but everybody knows it's my celebration."

3 Rogers and Palmer are now teammates at Chelsea and could do a combined celebration Credit: Getty Images - Getty

Now that Rogers has joined Palmer at Chelsea, the debate seems like it's going to continue to rumble on.

But Palmer isn't backing down, and now that he has a trademark on the celebration, he feels it's solely his now.



Although he has admitted he's up for doing a combined 'cold' move, saying: "I have trademarked the celebration…so if Morgan tries to do anything, bailiffs at his door.

"Jokes aside, we’ll probably do the celebration together."

Sports.title: How many Premier League managerial changes have there been this summer?
Sports.content:
How many Premier League managerial changes have there been this summer?

The Premier League has had a managerial shake-up for next season, with nine clubs making a change in the dugout.

Including the three promoted sides, half the division will have managers competing in the Premier League for the first time with their respective clubs.

9 Pep Guardiola bid farewell to Manchester City in May after a decade at the club Credit: Getty

Pep Guardiola decided to leave Manchester City at the end of last season after winning 20 major trophies with the side.

The longest-serving manager is now Mikel Arteta, who has served as the Arsenal boss for over six years, and will be the only Premier League-winning manager on the touchline.

Chelsea and Manchester United made big decisions at the end of last season and have spent the summer rebuilding with their new head coaches at the helm.

However, some clubs like Newcastle have lost their manager amid pre-season preparations and have precious time to prepare ahead of the new campaign.

Manchester City - Enzo Maresca

Guardiola's ten-year reign at City ended ahead of the final day of the 2024/25 season.

Enzo Maresca eventually replaced the Spaniard, having previously spent time at the club as a youth coach.

The Italian manager left Chelsea in hostile circumstances in January following the Blues' FIFA Club World Cup win, despite having three-and-a-half years left on his contract.

His coaching style has been heavily influenced by Guardiola, and he will want to guide the club through a turbulent transition following the departures of experienced squad members like John Stones, Nathan Ake, and Bernardo Silva.

The 46-year-old has shown he can win trophies despite his relatively short career, having previously guided the Leicester City to the Championship title.

9 Man United have been on an upwards trajectory since Michael Carrick's interim appointment in January Credit: Getty

Manchester United - Michael Carrick

After the sacking of Ruben Amorim, Michael Carrick was put in charge of the side on an interim basis.

The 45-year-old made it impossible for the Old Trafford hierarchy not to sign him permanently after securing Champions League football for next season.

Since taking charge in January, Carrick won more points per game (2.29) than any other Premier League manager.

His first full-time managerial role was spent at Middlesborough, where he reached the 2022/23 playoffs and the EFL Cup semi-finals the following year.

He signed a two-year contract to remain as boss in May, with United's win at Brighton marking his first official game as permanent manager.

9 New Liverpool boss Iraola is looking to re-shape the club's attack Credit: AFP

Liverpool - Andoni Iraola

Arne Slot was expected to continue as Liverpool head coach after eventually securing Champions League qualification for next season.

However, the Liverpool hierarchy released a statement following a disappointing fifth-place finish, stating: "Change is necessary in order for the club to keep moving forward."

The Reds decided to appoint Andoni Iraola following his wave of success with Bournemouth, having guided the Cherries to their first-ever European finish last year.

He took his old side on an 18-match unbeaten run to finish in sixth spot, with the Spaniard employing a fast-paced style that heavily relies on athletic players to press and transition.

Similarly to Maresca at City, Iraola joins the Merseyside club at a time of change, with legends like Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson having left in the summer.

9 The Chelsea role will be Alonso's third as a manager Credit: Getty

Chelsea - Xabi Alonso

Xabi Alonso was chosen by Chelsea as the permanent successor to Liam Rosenior, who was sacked in April only three months after he took over from Maresca.

The Liverpool legend is no stranger to English football but he is now set to begin his Premier League managerial career this season with the Blues.

He made his first-team debut in the dugout at Bayer Leverkusen, where he won the club their first-ever Bundesliga title in his first full term in charge without losing a single league game.

A year later, he landed the Real Madrid job, yet failed to replicate his success in La Liga.

Alonso's tenure lasted only eight months before he stepped down following a difficult run of results, prior to being announced as Chelsea boss for the 2026/27 season.

The 44-year-old saw most of his success come with a back-three formation, and he is expected to revert to that system at Stamford Bridge.

Since arriving at the club, he sanctioned a British-record move for Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117million to signal his high ambitions for the upcoming campaign.

9 German coach Matthias Jaissle is set for Newcastle Credit: AFP

Newcastle - Matthias Jaissle

Matthias Jaissle is the man backed to replace Eddie Howe at Newcastle following his shock exit.

Former Bournemouth manager Howe came under pressure after a poor season, seeing Newcastle finish 12th in the Premier League.

Jaissle is a two-time Asian Champions League winner with Al Ahli - a club owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, like Newcastle.

Since the 38-year-old arrived in Saudi Arabia, his team has played 138 matches, winning 92, drawing 21, and losing 25.

His tactics have been heavily influenced by the Red Bull coaching model, with his sides built around aggressive high pressing and intense counter-attack.

His coaching style could be ideally suited to Newcastle, who have built a squad around intensity and athleticism.

9 It will be Rose's first managerial job in the Premier League Credit: Getty

Bournemouth - Marco Rose

Marco Rose will be Bournemouth's new head coach next season after Iraola confirmed at the end of the campaign that he was leaving the south coast.

The German spent the majority of his playing career at Mainz 05 under Jurgen Klopp.

He also made his managerial breakthrough at the club as he took over their second team as player/assistant coach in 2010.

Three years later, he became Under-16s head coach at RB Salzburg in Austria before being named head coach of the first team in 2017.

Rose won back-to-back league titles and did not lose a home match during his two-year tenure.

He returned to Germany and oversaw Borussia Monchengladbach and Borussia Dortmund, securing Champions League at both clubs.

He eventually joined RB Leipzig and won the DFB-Pokal in 2023.

9 Arbeloa will be looking to guide Fulham to a top half finish for the first time since 2023 Credit: Getty

Fulham - Alvaro Arbeloa

Nine years after he last played in the Premier League, Alvaro Arbeloa will return as Fulham’s head coach.

After spending five years at the club, Marco Silva decided not to renew his contract at the London-based club, opting instead for a new challenge at Benfica.

As a player, Arbeloa helped Liverpool reach the Champions League final before winning La Liga, two Copa del Rey trophies and becoming a European champion with Real Madrid.

After retiring, he took charge of Real Madrid’s Under-19s, then their B team, before becoming interim head coach of the seniors in January 2026.

They reached the Champions League quarter-finals and finished second in LaLiga, but he stepped down at the end of the season before signing his contract at Craven Cottage.

9 Pierre Sage is looking to make his mark at Conference League winners Crystal Palace Credit: Getty

Crystal Palace - Pierre Sage

Pierre Sage faces the difficult task of replacing one of Crystal Palace's greatest-ever managers in Oliver Glasner.

Sage did not play professional football.

He got his break at Lyon when he was named interim manager of the first team and guided them to Europa League qualification, earning him the job on a permanent basis.

After leaving the club in January 2025, he was appointed at RC Lens that summer.

He led the club to their first Coupe de France trophy and secured qualification for the Champions League.

The 47-year-old's success caught the Eagles' attention following the open vacancy at Selhurst Park.

9 Glasner has revealed Forest had accepted Elliott Anderson would leave the club when he was appointed Credit: Getty

Nottingham Forest - Oliver Glasner

Forest suddenly announced the departure of Vitor Pereira - despite the club previously intending to extend his contract earlier this summer.

Glasner achieved major success at Palace, delivering trophies in back-to-back seasons.

He secured the south London club their first-ever major trophy by winning the FA Cup in 2025, followed by the Conference League.

However, after his contract expired, he decided not to sign an extension in order to pursue a new challenge.

Though Glasner insisted his decision was made prior to the transfer window, he grew visibly frustrated with the club's hierarchy over squad management.

He publicly expressed feeling abandoned following the high-profile January sales of club captain Marc Guehi to Manchester City and Eberechi Eze to Arsenal.

Meanwhile, Glasner already seems to be backed financially at Forest following the arrival of talented midfielder Xaver Schlager, whom Glasner previously worked with earlier in his career.

Sports.title: FIFA hit with another devastating blow just hours after doubling down on controversial plans
Sports.content:
FIFA hit with another devastating blow just hours after doubling down on controversial plans

The Asian Football Confederation has become the latest to turn on FIFA, which has doubled down on its plans to sell World Cup stakes.

Football's governing body has caused a civil war within the game after Gianni Infantino’s controversial scheme emerged this week.

3 FIFA president Gianni Infantino has publicly backed the controversial plan

The 56-year-old intends to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), in plans that could see shares in their biggest tournaments, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup, sold off to the highest bidder.

Infantino would be lined up to run FFE as its commissioner when his final FIFA presidency ends in 2031, assuming he is re-elected, which could then potentially see him earn tens of millions of pounds.

His plans have caused widespread criticism, with UEFA nations unanimously agreeing to a boycott if these schemes go ahead.

CONCACAF have also 'rejected the proposal', with the Asian Football Confederation now calling for FIFA to 'undertake an urgent review of its governance' in the latest devastating blow.

A statement read: “The AFC stands in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF in expressing serious concerns over FIFA’s proposal to introduce private investment into FIFA's flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE.

“The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a FIFA World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game. Football should never have been placed in such a position.”

Hours before the AFC spoke out, FIFA doubled down on its plans and blamed ‘incorrect media reports’ for ‘disrupting’ the consultation process.

FIFA hits back as UEFA plan to boycott

In a statement released on Friday morning, FIFA said: "We have heard the feedback provided by the respective confederations in relation to the proposed establishment of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) and would like to address the issues that have surfaced since the initial media reporting on Tuesday.

3 Infantino is even being doubted by his closest allies Credit: Getty

"We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation.

⁠"Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

"FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all FIFA Member Associations (MAs) have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of FIFA or football itself.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain.

"Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification, but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world.

"Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA."

As per FIFA's proposal FFE would move FIFA’s commercial and operational event delivery activities into a subsidiary organisation that FIFA would own and control permanently.

⁠The commercial value created would be shared among all 211 MAs, enabling each MA to make meaningful investments in football in their respective countries.

⁠Under the proposal, each MA would receive USD 20 million of FIFA Forward Development funding over the next four years (2027-2030), irrespective of its individual support.

⁠This increased funding would come from the additional revenues generated by FFE through the more effective management of FIFA’s commercial operations, for the benefit of all MAs.

⁠The FIFA Fast Forward Programme is a one-off development funding of an additional USD 20 million per MA – participation would be fully voluntary for all MAs should the FFE proposal proceed – and would be financed by external investment without ceding control or altering FIFA’s governance structure in any way.

⁠Without the support of the majority of MAs, FIFA's commercial activities would remain unchanged. FFE would not be established.

These components represent the starting point of the consultation process and are open for discussion as part of that process. This can include approval, rejection or amendment in their entirety or individually.

FIFA add that these so-called principles 'underpin the FFE proposal', yet talkSPORT has learned some of Infantino's closest allies from within the organisation are opposed to the plans.

Private investors holding minority stakes would allow them to have a say in broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing, and licensing decisions related to the World Cup.

With the idea of further raising revenue under such measures, the World Cup could be expanded to 64 teams, fans could be priced out of attending games, and Arsene Wenger's widely shunned proposal to make the tournament biennial could be revitalised.

FFE's lead investor is also expected to be Thrive Eternal, a private investment fund established by Joshua Kushner - whose brother Jared is the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.

3 Infantino had already been under pressure for his relationship with the Trump administration Credit: Getty

FIFA president Infantino has already come under mounting scrutiny for his close personal relationship with Trump.

The 80-year-old was awarded the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize during the group stage draw for the World Cup last December.

During the tournament itself, Trump then called Infantino to review the red card issued to USMNT striker Folarin Balogun, which in turn led to the latter's one-match ban being suspended for a year.

The landmark intervention has led to the Norwegian FA revealing its intention to make a formal complaint to FIFA's ethics committee.

Balogun's red card has since been linked with potential betting irregularities, while a US lawmaker has requested that Infantino appear before the House Judiciary Committee.

Infantino has responded to the increasingly escalating criticism of him in typical fashion - by accusing people of 'spreading hate'.

It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA’s duty as the custodian of world football.

This is not a “democratic decision”, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.

"This model has no place in world football. Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return.

"Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

The FA meanwhile have said: "We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view.

"We oppose FIFA’s plans - the FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will."

Sports.title: AC Milan left devastated as legendary defender Franco Baresi dies aged 66
Sports.content:
Legendary AC Milan defender Franco Baresi has died, aged 66.

The Rossoneri confirmed the tragic news on Friday morning, one day after clarifying premature reports surrounding Baresi's death.

4 Baresi was named AC Milan's 'Player of the Century' in 1999 Credit: Getty

Baresi is widely considered one of the greatest players in history after a 20-year career in which he played only for Milan and Italy.

Across the 70s, 80s and 90s, the 5ft 9ins centre-back redefined the art of defending with his outstanding reading of the game and footballing intelligence.

His iconic No.6 shirt remains retired at the San Siro after he captained one of the great Italian football sides to three European Cups and six Serie A titles.

"The entire history of AC Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi," the club wrote on social media.

"His example and integrity will be forever etched into the Club's DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is.

"The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi's family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own."

In a separate post on their website, Milan added: "Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan, is incredibly difficult.

"But everyone at the Club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi's memory. We must be strong and gather every bit of energy, even at this saddest of times.

"We lost Franco only a few months after his last public appearance in a packed San Siro, at the Milan Winter Olympics opening ceremony, an event on the world stage he helped make unforgettable.

"In memory of Franco, we stand united, knowing he'll guide and push us throughout our Rossoneri journey. Forever. Because Baresi is forever."

4 Baresi led one of Italian football's greatest-ever teams to European glory three times Credit: Getty

Baresi worked as an honorary vice-president at Milan following his retirement in 1997, although he suffered health problems in recent years.

He underwent surgery in August 2025 to remove a pulmonary nodule and had been undergoing immunotherapy treatment.

Tributes

The late Diego Maradona once described Baresi as his toughest opponent.

Meanwhile, our very own Ray Wilkins, who passed away in 2018, said the Italy icon was his greatest ever teammate.

Inter Milan have led the tributes on Friday, showing their respect for a legendary rival.

The club wrote: "Farewell to Franco Baresi, protagonist of the great clashes in the Milan Derby and one of the figures who most defined the history of the rivalry.

4 Milan's No.6 shirt forever belongs to Baresi and nobody else Credit: Getty

"Captain, team man, and flag bearer of AC Milan, he lived every matchup with Inter between competition and respect, within a challenge that wrote unforgettable pages of Italian soccer.

"President Giuseppe Marotta and all of FC Internazionale Milano stand in solidarity with the Baresi family, brother Beppe, and AC Milan in this moment of grief."

Fellow Serie A giants Juventus paid their own classy tribute.

Juve wrote: "There are people who, with their talent, enter history.

"And others who, with their humanity, remain there forever. Franco Baresi was both. Class, style, leadership, and respect on and off the field.

"An example for generations of players and fans, loved and admired by all football enthusiasts. His memory will live on forever.

4 Baresi used his intelligence and reading of the game better than perhaps anyone in history Credit: Getty

"Juventus Football Club stands in solidarity with the Baresi family and AC Milan in this moment of profound sorrow."

Reacting to the news on the talkSPORT Breakfast Show, presenter Andy Goldstein reflected on a sad loss for the game.

"My goodness, what a player," Goldstein said.

"He was absolutely fantastic. Such a loss, not just to football, but the Italian footballing world.

"He was a genius of a player."

Sports.title: FIFA's World Cup plot looks dead in the water as Asian Federation stand with UEFA and CONCACAF to deny Gianni Infantino a majority - but deluded president vows to plough on with his controversial plan
Sports.content:
FIFA's World Cup plot looks dead in the water as Asian Federation stand with UEFA and CONCACAF to deny Gianni Infantino a majority - but deluded president vows to plough on with his controversial plan

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Gianni Infantino's divisive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup appears to be dead after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) joined UEFA and CONCACAF in opposing the plot.

Overnight, FIFA issued a statement, doubling down on plans to sell £3.1 billion in shares for FIFA tournaments after UEFA announced a boycott of competitions and CONCACAF - the North, Central, American and Caribbean federation - opposed the plans.

But the AFC has now chosen to stand with their intercontinental counterparts, leaving Infantino's project - and potentially his FIFA presidency - facing a terminal threat.

136 FIFA members are now publicly opposed to the proposals, bringing the dissidents above the required 106 threshold to block the plans.

In a statement, the AFC said: 'The AFC stands in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF in expressing serious concerns over FIFA's proposal to introduce private investment into FIFA's flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE.

'The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a FIFA World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game. Football should never have been placed in such a position.

Gianni Infantino's controversial plan to sell off the World Cup appears to be dead in the water after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) joined UEFA and CONCACAF in opposing the plot

'Against this backdrop, and in light of the clear positions expressed by UEFA and CONCACAF, as well as the unprecedented divisions that have emerged across the football world, the AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.

'The FIFA World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world's leading football nations.

'Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered.

'While the immediate debate centres on FFE, the AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal.

'Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed.

'While the AFC notes FIFA's latest clarification on the proposal, the central concerns surrounding governance, institutional process and meaningful consultation remain unanswered.

'A proposal of such significance, with the potential to affect the commercial, sporting and strategic future of world football, must not emerge through processes that leave Confederations, Member Associations (MAs) and even FIFA's own governing bodies, including the FIFA Council, feeling sidelined.

'The primary objective for world football must be to ensure that decisions of such magnitude are being developed through processes that are anchored on transparency and command the confidence of the football community.

'This is not the first occasion where major stakeholders have been confronted with significant initiatives after the direction of travel appears to have already been determined.

'Such an approach undermines confidence in FIFA's governance framework and diminishes the authority of its statutory bodies.

'No subsequent consultation process, however well-intentioned, can replace early engagement with the appropriate FIFA bodies and the football family.

'The AFC believes this moment must become a catalyst for strengthening institutional reform. While every FIFA MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote.

'It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.

'Accordingly, the AFC calls upon FIFA to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by FIFA's statutory bodies.

'The FIFA World Cup, and the game itself, belong to the entire global football family. Their future must always be shaped collectively, through institutions that reflect the voices of all Confederations and MAs.'

The AFC's statement criticises FIFA's clarification of their proposals released on Friday morning, where they blamed the media for misconstruing their plans and made a dig at UEFA for holding FIFA to account.

FIFA said: 'We have heard the feedback provided by the respective confederations in relation to the proposed establishment of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) and would like to address the issues that have surfaced since the initial media reporting on Tuesday.

'We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation.

⁠'Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

'FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all FIFA Member Associations (MAs) have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of FIFA or football itself.

'Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain.

'Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world. Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA.'

They continued by outlining the plans, subject to consultation with member nations.

There is frustration across the international football landscape, however, that such proposals have been unilaterally developed - with proposed investors already lined up - in complete secrecy despite an eventual 'consultation'.

UEFA nations are boycotting all FIFA competitions so long as the proposals remain on the table. All 55 UEFA nations met virtually on Thursday, with more than 40 federations providing testimony.

Daily Mail Sport were told associations expressed ‘outrage’ on the call with ‘total unanimity’ against the proposal, before deciding to abstain from FIFA competitions.

Daily Mail Sport also understands there is growing opposition to Infantino's presidency, with CONCACAF nations losing - or having already lost - confidence in the Swiss football administrator.

UEFA and their member associations are yet to be drawn on that matter. Infantino is seeking a fourth term as FIFA president next year.

One international football insider told Daily Mail Sport: ‘UEFA’s response is at the nuclear button end of the spectrum, which is impressive. We thought Infantino would survive the Trump refereeing intervention - but he has overreached this time.'

In a statement, UEFA said: 'UEFA and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA's proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors.

'The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

'It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football.

'National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football's greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a 'democratic decision', but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

'But our opposition goes far beyond process.

'The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure. From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.

'This model has no place in world football. Football's future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return. Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

'Europe's position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation.

'As a result of today's discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.

'Nobody should be in any doubt: UEFA and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.

'There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments.

'Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.’

An FA spokeswoman added: 'We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose FIFA's plans - the FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will.’

Concacaf later added: 'Concacaf is a confederation united by the love of our game, where football comes first. Guided by this philosophy over the past ten years we have built, from the ground up, an organisation founded on service, transparent governance, and the long-term stewardship of football.

'History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values.

'With this in mind, Concacaf today convened a meeting of the presidents of its 41 Member Associations, together with its President, Council members, and its FIFA Council members, to discuss a proposal developed and presented by the FIFA President to establish 'FIFA Forward Enterprise' and sell interests in the FIFA World Cup to private investors.

'During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies. In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programs following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.

'The discussion reinforced the need for greater transparency and proper governance.

'For these reasons, Concacaf and its 41 Member Associations have: Rejected the proposal; Tasked their FIFA Council Members with engaging FIFA to determine how existing FIFA reserves could be used to increase FIFA Forward funding for football development across our region; and Tasked their FIFA Council Members with instructing the FIFA President to ensure that any matter follows the proper governance processes via staff and FIFA Council, in accordance with the FIFA Statutes.

'Through these actions, Concacaf reaffirms that football's future - and its greatest asset - must remain in the hands of our football family.'
