The Influence-Peddling Charge Explained

Separate from the corporate reshuffle, Ricardo Roa faces a legal challenge. On March 11, 2026, Colombia’s Attorney General’s Office (Fiscalía) charged him with a crime.

The charge is “tráfico de influencias de servidor público,” which translates to influence-peddling by a public servant. All charges are allegations, and Roa is presumed innocent.

Authorities are investigating the purchase of an apartment in Bogotá. The probe is examining a possible connection between the property and Ecopetrol contracts.

Roa has publicly stated he will face the justice system. He also pledged not to leave the country while the legal process unfolds.

The Attorney General’s Office has not released further details on the specific contracts under review. The investigation remains ongoing.

Political Context for International Investors

Ricardo Roa was not a traditional oil executive. He managed Gustavo Petro’s successful 2022 presidential campaign before his appointment to Ecopetrol.

President Petro appointed Roa to lead the state-controlled company as part of his agenda to transform Colombia’s energy policy. The leadership change is closely watched by markets.

Ecopetrol accounts for a large share of Colombia‘s exports and government revenue. Its ADRs are widely held by international funds tracking emerging markets.

The board and management changes create a new landscape for the company’s strategy. Investors will look for signals on exploration, production, and the energy transition.

The acting president, Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra, now leads the company during this transition. The appointment of a permanent president will be a critical next step.

What Comes Next for Ecopetrol

The company must now stabilise its leadership team. The departure of the energy transition vice-president adds a layer of strategic uncertainty.

Ecopetrol’s traditional oil and gas business remains its core revenue driver. International crude prices and operational efficiency will heavily influence near-term results.

The legal case against Roa will proceed independently in Colombia’s courts. The company itself has not been charged with any wrongdoing in this matter.

For the investment community, governance standards and legal transparency are paramount. The dual events of the reshuffle and the criminal charge will require careful monitoring.

Ecopetrol’s next earnings report and investor calls will likely provide the first official clues about the board’s new strategic direction under Henao Cardona’s chairmanship.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Ricardo Roa leave Ecopetrol?

Ricardo Roa left the presidency of Ecopetrol on July 30, 2026, as part of a wider board and management reshuffle. The company also saw the departure of its board chair and two vice-presidents.

What is the legal charge against Ricardo Roa?

On March 11, 2026, Colombia’s Attorney General’s Office charged Roa with influence-peddling by a public servant. The charge is an allegation linked to a Bogotá apartment purchase and possible Ecopetrol contracts. Roa is presumed innocent.

Who is leading Ecopetrol now?

Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra, the president’s first alternate, became acting president on July 31, 2026. Luis Felipe Henao Cardona is the new chair of the board of directors.

World.title: Florianopolis Convention Center Goes Private in 35-Year Deal
World.content:
Brazil · Santa Catarina

Key Facts —Asset Centro de Convenções de Florianópolis (CentroSul), the main convention center in Florianopolis, Santa Catarina state. —Term 35-year concession for management, operation, commercial exploitation, and revitalization works. —Minimum Bid R$16.5 million (~US$3.05 million) as a one-time initial payment, plus an annual fee of R$250,000 (~US$46,300). —Award Criterion The highest initial payment proposal wins the public bidding process. —Timeline Proposals are due September 14, 2026. The public bidding session is scheduled for September 18, 2026, at the B3 stock exchange in São Paulo.

The municipality of Florianopolis published a bidding notice on July 28, 2026, to hand the Florianopolis convention center to a private operator. The 35-year concession covers the CentroSul venue and requires a minimum initial payment of R$16.5 million (~US$3.05 million).

Downtown Florianopolis, Santa Catarina. The city is privatizing its convention center. (Photo: internal archive)

The Asset: CentroSul in Brazil’s ‘Magic Island’

The Centro de Convenções de Florianópolis, known locally as CentroSul, is the primary events hub in the capital of Santa Catarina state. Florianopolis, often called ‘Floripa’ or the ‘Magic Island,’ is a top destination for international tourists and digital nomads in southern Brazil.

The venue hosts business conferences, cultural events, and trade shows. The city government aims to modernize the space without draining public funds.

Financial Structure and Bid Rules

The concession model requires a private partner to pay a one-time initial fee, known as an outorga. The floor for this payment is set at R$16.5 million (~US$3.05 million).

Beyond the upfront sum, the winner must pay a fixed annual fee of R$250,000 (~US$46,300) to the municipality throughout the 35-year contract. The operator will also take on mandatory revitalization and renovation works.

The award criterion is strictly financial. The bidder that offers the highest initial payment, above the R$16.5 million floor, wins the contract. This straightforward rule reduces legal disputes and speeds up the selection process.

The Florianopolis skyline. The 35-year concession opens to bids in September. (Photo: internal archive)

Timeline and Bidding Process

Interested companies must submit their proposals on September 14, 2026, between 10 a.m. and noon. The public bidding session will occur four days later, on September 18, 2026.

Both the delivery of proposals and the bidding session will take place at the headquarters of B3, the Brazilian stock exchange, in São Paulo. Holding the auction at B3 signals a push for transparency and attracts institutional investors familiar with capital markets.

The short window between the notice and the bid date suggests the municipality wants to close the deal quickly. International investors must move fast to conduct due diligence on the asset.

Why the Florianopolis Convention Center Matters for Investors

This concession is part of a broader Brazilian trend of monetizing public assets. Municipalities and states are increasingly turning to the private sector to operate airports, parks, and event spaces.

For an international investor, the CentroSul offers a monopoly-like position in a high-growth city. Florianopolis has a resilient economy driven by tourism, technology startups, and a booming real estate market.

The 35-year term provides a long runway to recoup the initial investment. The operator can generate revenue from event rentals, parking, food and beverage services, and commercial partnerships inside the venue.

However, the mandatory revitalization works add a capital expenditure layer that bidders must calculate carefully. The winning consortium will need to balance renovation costs against future revenue projections.

Impact on the Local Economy and Tourism

City officials expect the concession to boost the local economy by attracting larger national and international events. A modernized convention center can draw business travelers who spend more per day than leisure tourists.

The deal also removes a financial burden from the municipal budget. Instead of funding maintenance and upgrades, the city collects an annual fee and an upfront payment.

Local businesses, including hotels, restaurants, and transport services, stand to benefit from increased foot traffic. The revitalization mandate ensures the building does not deteriorate under private management.

Risks and Considerations for Bidders

The fixed annual payment of R$250,000 (~US$46,300) is a long-term obligation that must be paid regardless of the venue’s profitability. Bidders must stress-test their revenue models against seasonal fluctuations in the events market.

Currency risk is another factor for foreign investors. The concession operates entirely in Brazilian reais, and the exchange rate used for the minimum bid is approximately 5.4 reais per US dollar.

Competition from other venues in southern Brazil could also pressure margins. Still, Florianopolis’s strong brand as a lifestyle destination gives CentroSul a competitive edge that other cities struggle to match.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the minimum bid for the Florianopolis convention center concession?

The minimum initial payment is R$16.5 million, which equals approximately US$3.05 million at an exchange rate of 5.4 reais per dollar. The winner must also pay an annual fee of R$250,000 (~US$46,300).

When are the proposals due for the CentroSul concession?

Proposals must be delivered on September 14, 2026, between 10 a.m. and noon. The public bidding session is scheduled for September 18, 2026. Both events take place at the B3 stock exchange in São Paulo.

What does the 35-year concession include?

The contract covers the management, operation, and commercial exploitation of the CentroSul venue. The private operator must also complete mandatory revitalization and renovation works on the building.

World.title: Lulinha Investigation Opens Into Brazil President’s Son
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —Authorization STF Minister Andre Mendonca authorized the Federal Police inquiry on July 30, 2026. —Subject The probe targets Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, President Lula’s eldest son, known as ‘Lulinha’. —Allegation Suspected influence-peddling and corruption in medicinal-cannabis commercialization authorizations. —Alleged partners The inquiry cites an alleged partnership with Roberta Luchsinger and lobbyist Antonio Carlos Camilo Antunes. —Status Lulinha has not been charged and is presumed innocent; this is the opening of an investigation.

Lulinha investigation proceedings were formally authorized by Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court (STF) on Thursday, July 30, 2026, as Minister Andre Mendonca approved a Federal Police request to open an inquiry into Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, the eldest son of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

The Planalto Palace in Brasilia. Brazil’s Supreme Court cleared a police inquiry into President Lula’s eldest son. (Photo: internal archive)

STF Authorizes Inquiry

The Federal Police (PF) sent its formal request to the STF on Friday, July 24, 2026.

Minister Andre Mendonca reviewed the petition and authorized the investigation six days later, on July 30.

The inquiry will examine whether Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, widely known by the nickname ‘Lulinha’, allegedly acted as an intermediary for private interests seeking access to the presidential palace and the Ministry of Health.

The specific focus is the suspected intermediation of business deals in the medicinal-cannabis market, particularly products containing cannabidiol (CBD).

All allegations at this stage are suspicions presented by the Federal Police and have not been tested in court.

Scope of the Allegations

The Federal Police request cites an alleged partnership between Lulinha, businesswoman Roberta Luchsinger, and lobbyist Antonio Carlos Camilo Antunes.

Antunes is known by the nickname ‘Careca do INSS’, a reference to Brazil’s National Social Security Institute.

The trio allegedly acted on behalf of a company called ‘World Cannabis’, which is linked to Antunes.

Investigators suspect the group sought to influence Ministry of Health programs that authorize the commercialization of medicinal-cannabis products.

The suspected crimes under investigation include influence-peddling, known in Brazilian law as ‘tráfico de influência’, and potential corruption.

No formal charges have been filed against any of the individuals named in the inquiry.

Brazil’s seat of government in Brasilia. The inquiry is preliminary; no charges have been filed. (Photo: internal archive)

The Lulinha Investigation in Context

Fabio Luis Lula da Silva is the eldest of President Lula’s five children and has previously worked as a technology entrepreneur.

He has largely maintained a low public profile during his father’s third presidential term, which began in January 2023.

Investigations involving relatives of sitting Brazilian presidents are historically sensitive and carry significant political weight.

The opening of an inquiry does not imply wrongdoing or guilt under Brazilian law.

Legal experts emphasize that a Federal Police investigation is a preliminary step to determine whether sufficient evidence exists to bring formal charges.

Lulinha is presumed innocent, and his legal representatives have not yet issued a public statement on the matter.

Political and Electoral Landscape

The authorization comes as Brazil approaches the October 2026 presidential election, in which President Lula is widely expected to seek re-election.

Political analysts note that any investigation touching the presidential family will face intense scrutiny from both allies and opponents.

The STF, Brazil’s highest constitutional court, has played a central role in numerous high-profile corruption investigations over the past decade.

Minister Andre Mendonca, who authorized the inquiry, was appointed to the STF by former President Jair Bolsonaro in 2021.

Mendonca is a conservative jurist and former attorney general who has ruled on several politically sensitive cases.

The investigation will proceed under judicial secrecy, a standard practice in Brazilian criminal inquiries at this stage.

Medicinal-Cannabis Regulation in Brazil

Brazil’s medicinal-cannabis market has grown rapidly in recent years, with the National Health Surveillance Agency (Anvisa) authorizing several CBD-based products.

The Ministry of Health also manages programs that facilitate patient access to medicinal cannabis through the public health system, known as SUS.

Companies seeking to participate in these programs must navigate complex regulatory approvals, creating potential entry points for lobbyists and intermediaries.

The Federal Police’s interest in this sector suggests investigators are examining whether personal connections were allegedly used to fast-track or influence authorizations.

Brazil’s legal framework for medicinal cannabis remains a subject of legislative debate, with Congress considering broader cultivation and distribution laws.

Next Steps in the Inquiry

The Federal Police will now begin collecting documents, conducting interviews, and gathering evidence under the supervision of the STF.

There is no set timeline for the investigation, which could last months or longer depending on its complexity.

If investigators find sufficient evidence, they will forward their findings to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which decides whether to file formal charges.

Only after formal charges are accepted by the STF would Fabio Luis Lula da Silva become a defendant in a criminal case.

Until then, he remains an investigated person with full presumption of innocence guaranteed by Brazil’s 1988 Constitution.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Lulinha investigation about?

The Lulinha investigation is a Federal Police inquiry authorized by Brazil’s Supreme Court into suspected influence-peddling by Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, President Lula’s eldest son, related to medicinal-cannabis commercialization authorizations.

Has Fabio Luis Lula da Silva been charged with a crime?

No. He has not been charged with any crime. The STF has only authorized the opening of an investigation. Under Brazilian law, he is presumed innocent, and the inquiry will determine whether evidence supports any formal accusation.

Who authorized the investigation and why?

STF Minister Andre Mendonca authorized the inquiry on July 30, 2026, after reviewing a Federal Police request. The police suspect Lulinha allegedly acted as an intermediary for a company called World Cannabis in dealings with the Ministry of Health.

World.title: Cuba Private Sector Opens to 81 Activities as Economy Nears Collapse
World.content:
Cuba · Economy

Key Facts —Announcement date July 29, 2026, following parliamentary approval on June 18, 2026. —Activities opened Roughly 81 activities, including gas stations, pharmacies, nursing homes, ports, vehicle imports, renewable energy, and mining. —Capital allowed Both domestic and foreign private investment are permitted under the new framework. —Crisis context Five nationwide blackouts in 2026, plus shortages of food, fuel, water, and medicine, exacerbated by tightened US sanctions. —State-controlled sectors Healthcare, education, media, and defense remain exclusively under state operation.

Cuba private sector investment will be allowed in roughly 81 activities previously reserved exclusively for the state, the government announced on July 29, 2026, marking a historic shift for the island’s centrally planned economy as it teeters on the edge of collapse.

Classic cars pass Havana’s National Capitol. Cuba is opening dozens of sectors to private capital. (Photo: internal archive)

What Opened: From Gas Stations to Ports

The new package dismantles the state monopoly on a wide range of commercial and industrial activities. Gasoline distribution, including service stations, will now be open to private operators.

Pharmacies and optical services can be run by private capital, a significant change for a sector entirely in state hands for decades. Geriatric homes, or nursing homes, are also included, addressing an aging population with limited care options.

Transport infrastructure is a major focus. Passenger and cargo terminals, as well as port facilities, will be opened to private management and investment.

The measures also permit private vehicle imports, a business tightly controlled until now. In the energy and extractive sectors, renewable energy projects, plus oil and gas and mining operations, will be open under certain conditions.

The 176-Measure Market Package

Parliament approved the comprehensive 176-measure package on June 18, 2026. The July 29 announcement detailed the implementation of opening these roughly 81 activities to both national and foreign capital.

Analysts describe the move as a historic shift for Cuba’s Soviet-style command economy. It follows earlier, more limited openings for small and medium-sized private businesses, known locally as MSMEs or mipymes.

The government frames the package as a necessary update to save the economy, not an ideological surrender. However, the scale of the transfer of economic activity to the private sphere is unprecedented since the 1959 revolution.

Daily commerce in Cuba. The reforms cover gas stations, pharmacies, ports and energy. (Photo: internal archive)

Context: US Sanctions and a Deepening Crisis

The opening comes as Cuba faces one of its gravest economic crises in decades. The US economic embargo, in place since 1962, was significantly tightened in January 2026.

The Trump administration added a de facto oil blockade and further sanctions on Cuban firms and officials. These measures severely restricted the island’s ability to import fuel, pushing the economy toward collapse.

The impact on daily life has been severe. Cuba has suffered five nationwide blackouts so far in 2026. Chronic shortages of food, drinking water, fuel, and medicine have become the norm for millions of residents.

For an international reader, this means the state can no longer finance or manage the basic infrastructure of daily life. The private sector is being called in not just for growth, but for basic economic survival.

What Stays State-Controlled

The reforms do not signal a wholesale retreat of the state. The government was explicit that core social and political sectors will remain under exclusive state control.

Healthcare and education, long the pillars of the revolutionary system, will not be privatized. Media and defense also remain firmly in state hands.

This delineation creates a dual economy: a private sector allowed to operate in commercial and infrastructure activities, while the state retains its monopoly on social services, information, and security. The line appears designed to preserve the political model while offloading economic burdens.

Cuba Private Sector: A Forced Evolution

For foreign investors and expats watching Latin America, the move signals both opportunity and extreme risk. The legal framework for foreign capital in ports, energy, and mining is new, but the operating environment remains fraught with sanctions complications.

Any foreign company engaging with the new Cuba private sector must navigate US sanctions law, particularly the Helms-Burton Act, which can penalize foreign firms for trafficking in property confiscated after the revolution.

The domestic private sector, while gaining legal access to new industries, faces a population with almost no purchasing power. The success of these measures will depend on whether they can attract capital to rebuild infrastructure fast enough to halt the humanitarian crisis.

Frequently Asked Questions

What activities is Cuba opening to the private sector?

Cuba is opening roughly 81 activities, including gas stations, pharmacies, optical services, nursing homes, passenger and cargo terminals, port facilities, vehicle imports, renewable energy, and oil, gas, and mining operations.

Can foreign investors participate in Cuba’s new private sector openings?

Yes, the announced measures explicitly allow both domestic and foreign private capital to invest in the newly opened activities, though they must still navigate US sanctions risks.

Which sectors will remain under state control in Cuba?

The Cuban government has stated that healthcare, education, media, and defense will remain exclusively state-run and are not part of the private sector opening.

World.title: Lula Paraguay War Remark Triggers Diplomatic Summons
World.content:
Mercosur · Diplomacy

Key Facts —The Trigger Brazilian President Lula said Paraguay ‘decided to invade Brazil’ during a defense-policy event, referencing the 1864-70 War of the Triple Alliance. —Diplomatic Action Paraguay’s Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez Lezcano summoned Brazil’s ambassador in Asunción to formally reject the remarks and deliver a diplomatic note. —Historical Context Historians dispute Lula’s framing, noting the war escalated after Brazil’s 1864 military intervention in Uruguay, which was allied with Paraguay at the time. —De-escalation A meeting between foreign ministers in Lima led to a phone call between Presidents Santiago Peña and Lula, with Paraguay handling the complaint with ‘strategic prudence.’ —Mercosur Strain The diplomatic row adds tension inside Mercosur, South America’s leading trade bloc, where both Brazil and Paraguay are founding members.

Lula Paraguay diplomatic tensions flared on Tuesday when Paraguay’s government summoned Brazil’s ambassador in Asunción. The move came after Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva declared that Paraguay ‘decided to invade Brazil,’ reopening a painful chapter over the deadliest interstate conflict in South American history.

The Palacio de los Lopez, seat of Paraguay’s government in Asuncion. (Photo: internal archive)

What Lula Said

Speaking at a defense-policy event, President Lula addressed Brazil’s military posture by invoking a historical reference that immediately drew scrutiny. He stated, ‘We like peace, but we cannot forget that, one day, Paraguay decided to invade Brazil,’ adding that the conflict also reached Uruguay and Argentina.

The remarks referred directly to the War of the Triple Alliance, a conflict fought from 1864 to 1870 that pitted Paraguay against a coalition of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. For many Paraguayans, Lula’s framing oversimplified a complex historical event that remains a cornerstone of national identity and collective memory.

Paraguay’s Formal Diplomatic Response

Paraguay’s Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez Lezcano acted swiftly, announcing that the government would summon Brazil’s ambassador to formally reject the remarks. The diplomat was called to the Foreign Ministry in Asunción, where officials delivered a formal diplomatic note expressing the country’s strong disagreement.

Vice President Pedro Alliana joined the foreign minister in the official démarche, signaling the high level of government attention the issue received. Minister Ramírez Lezcano stressed that while Paraguay seeks constructive bilateral ties, ‘Paraguay’s dignity is not negotiable.’

The Asuncion skyline. Paraguay summoned Brazil’s ambassador over Lula’s remark. (Photo: internal archive)

Lula Paraguay and the Disputed History

The historical dispute behind the diplomatic row is far from settled among scholars. Many historians challenge Lula’s assertion that Paraguay unilaterally decided to invade Brazil, pointing instead to a chain of regional interventions that escalated the conflict.

The war’s immediate trigger is often traced to Brazil’s 1864 military intervention in Uruguay, a country then allied with Paraguay under President Francisco Solano López. López viewed the Brazilian incursion as a threat to the regional balance of power, leading him to seize a Brazilian vessel and order troops into the contested Mato Grosso territory.

What followed was a catastrophic six-year war that devastated Paraguay. Historical estimates suggest the country lost a significant portion of its population, with some demographic studies indicating mortality rates above 50 percent. The conflict reshaped borders and left a deep scar on Paraguay’s national psyche, making any simplified narrative of war guilt a highly sensitive matter in Asunción.

De-escalation Through Direct Diplomacy

Within hours of the diplomatic summons, both governments moved to de-escalate the situation. Foreign Minister Ramírez Lezcano revealed that he met his Brazilian counterpart, Mauro Vieira, in person in Lima, Peru, where the two diplomats discussed the controversy directly.

That meeting paved the way for a phone call between Paraguay’s President Santiago Peña and President Lula. According to Ramírez Lezcano, President Peña handled the complaint ‘with strategic prudence,’ balancing the need to defend Paraguay’s historical position with the broader bilateral relationship.

The rapid back-channel communication underscored the institutional maturity of both nations. Neither government signaled an intention to let the historical disagreement derail ongoing cooperation on trade, infrastructure, or security matters.

Mercosur and Regional Implications

The diplomatic spat carries weight beyond bilateral ties because both countries are founding members of Mercosur, South America’s flagship trade bloc. The grouping, which also includes Argentina and Uruguay, has faced internal strains over trade policy and political alignment in recent years.

A public disagreement over historical memory between two of the bloc’s largest economies adds an unwelcome layer of friction. Analysts note that while the immediate crisis appears contained, it highlights the enduring sensitivity of the War of the Triple Alliance in Paraguayan politics and diplomacy.

For foreign investors and expatriates following Latin America, the episode illustrates how historical narratives can suddenly surface in regional diplomacy. Paraguay’s firm but measured response suggests the government in Asunción will continue to push back against what it views as inaccurate historical portrayals, even from its largest Mercosur partner.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did President Lula say about Paraguay?

Lula stated at a defense event that ‘one day, Paraguay decided to invade Brazil,’ referencing the War of the Triple Alliance. He added that the conflict also involved Uruguay and Argentina.

How did Paraguay respond to Lula’s remarks?

Paraguay summoned Brazil’s ambassador in Asunción, delivered a formal diplomatic note of rejection, and had its vice president join the foreign minister in the démarche. The government called the remarks an inaccurate framing of history.

What was the War of the Triple Alliance?

The War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870) was a South American conflict in which Paraguay fought against a coalition of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. It was the deadliest interstate war in the region’s history and devastated Paraguay’s population and economy.

World.title: Panama Canal Draft Cut Again as El Niño Threatens Water
World.content:
Panama · Shipping

Key Facts —New Draft Limit The maximum authorized draft drops to 49.0 feet on July 24, 2026, and further to 48.5 feet from August 15, 2026. —Reason Strengthening El Niño conditions are forecast to bring significantly lower rainfall to the Panama Canal Watershed, reducing water levels in Gatun Lake. —Transit Numbers Unchanged The Panama Canal Authority has not reduced the number of daily ship transits, maintaining its May 2026 decision to rule out transit restrictions through December 31. —Key Distinction Draft restrictions limit how deep a vessel sits in the water and thus its cargo load, while transit restrictions limit the number of ships passing through daily. —Shipping Impact Some ocean carriers are preparing to implement surcharges on trans-Pacific trade routes in response to the new weight limitations.

Panama Canal draft limits are being tightened again, with the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) announcing a two-step reduction that will bring the maximum authorized depth for vessels down to 48.5 feet by mid-August 2026.

The Miraflores Locks on the Panama Canal. The waterway is lowering draft limits as El Nino strengthens. (Photo: internal archive)

How the New Panama Canal Draft Limits Work

The ACP confirmed that the maximum authorized draft will be lowered to 49.0 feet (14.94 meters) in Tropical Fresh Water (TFW), effective July 24, 2026. A second cut will follow on August 15, 2026, reducing the limit further to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters).

These figures represent the deepest point a vessel’s hull can sit below the waterline while transiting the canal. The change directly limits how much cargo a ship can carry, as heavier loads push the vessel deeper into the water.

Why Gatun Lake is the Critical Factor

The entire Panama Canal system depends on fresh water from Gatun Lake, a vast artificial reservoir in central Panama that feeds the locks and sustains operations. Every time a ship passes through the locks, millions of gallons of fresh water are released from the lake into the sea.

Gatun Lake also supplies drinking water to Panama City, the nation’s capital and home to nearly half the population. The ACP must balance the competing demands of global maritime trade and domestic water security.

The lake’s water level is entirely dependent on rainfall across the Panama Canal Watershed, a sprawling catchment area of tropical forest. When rainfall drops, the lake shrinks, and the canal’s operational depth decreases accordingly.

The draft restrictions are a direct conservation measure. By requiring ships to float higher and carry less weight, the ACP reduces the volume of water needed for each transit, preserving Gatun Lake’s reserves for the dry months ahead.

A container ship transits the Panama Canal. Draft limits cap how deeply loaded vessels can be. (Photo: internal archive)

The 2023-24 Drought Precedent

The current situation echoes a severe drought that gripped the canal during the 2023-2024 period, which was also driven by an El Niño weather pattern. That crisis forced the ACP to slash daily transits from the normal 36-38 ships down to as few as 22 per day.

Ship queues stretched for weeks, and some vessels carrying millions of dollars in cargo were forced to wait or reroute around South America. The disruption snarled global supply chains and pushed up freight rates on key routes between Asia and the US East Coast.

The memory of that crisis is why shippers and global trade analysts are watching the current El Niño forecasts with heightened concern. The ACP’s early move to tighten draft limits is a direct lesson learned from that experience, aiming to avoid a repeat of the drastic transit cuts.

Draft vs. Transit: A Crucial Distinction for Shippers

A critical point for the shipping industry is that the ACP is not cutting the number of daily transits. In May 2026, the authority explicitly ruled out transit restrictions for the remainder of the year, and that position holds despite the new draft limits.

Draft restrictions and transit restrictions are fundamentally different tools. A draft limit controls how much a single ship can carry, while a transit limit controls how many ships can pass through the canal each day.

By tightening draft but not transits, the ACP is prioritizing the continued flow of vessel traffic. Shippers can still get their slots through the canal’s booking and reservation system, but they will have to sail with lighter loads.

For a large Neopanamax container ship, a reduction of one foot in draft can mean carrying hundreds of fewer containers. This forces shipping lines to either leave cargo behind or split loads across more vessels, increasing operational costs.

Surcharges and the Cost for Global Trade

Several major ocean carriers are already preparing to pass these higher costs on to customers. Shipping lines are announcing fresh surcharges for cargo moving on trans-Pacific routes that rely on the Panama Canal crossing.

These weight-limit surcharges are designed to compensate for the lost revenue from carrying fewer containers per voyage. Importers and exporters moving goods between Asia and the US East and Gulf Coasts will feel the impact directly on their freight invoices.

The Panama Canal handles a significant share of world maritime trade, serving as the primary shortcut for vessels traveling between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Any sustained restriction on cargo capacity ripples through commodity markets, retail supply chains, and energy shipments.

The canal is particularly vital for US grain exports, South American fruit and copper shipments, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) tankers moving from the US Gulf Coast to Asia. Heavier bulk carriers and fully loaded gas tankers are among the vessel types most sensitive to draft reductions.

Outlook for the 2026 El Niño Season

Updated meteorological forecasts indicate that the current El Niño pattern is strengthening, with a high probability of below-normal rainfall across the Panama Canal Watershed for the remainder of the year. The ACP’s two-step draft reduction is a proactive response to this outlook.

The authority has stated it will continue to monitor water levels and weather projections, leaving the door open for further adjustments if conditions worsen. For now, the focus remains on conserving water while keeping the canal open for business at full transit capacity.

For international investors and expatriates following Latin American trade infrastructure, the situation underscores the Panama Canal’s acute vulnerability to climate variability. The waterway’s operational health remains a barometer for the reliability of one of the world’s most critical trade arteries.

Connected Coverage

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new Panama Canal draft limit for August 2026?

The maximum authorized draft will be 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) in Tropical Fresh Water, effective from August 15, 2026. This follows an initial reduction to 49.0 feet on July 24, 2026.

Is the Panama Canal reducing the number of daily ship transits?

No. The Panama Canal Authority has not reduced the number of daily transits. It ruled out transit restrictions in May 2026, and that decision remains in place. Only the maximum draft, or vessel depth, is being restricted.

Why is the Panama Canal draft being reduced?

The reduction is due to a strengthening El Niño weather pattern, which is forecast to bring significantly lower rainfall to the Panama Canal Watershed. Less rain means lower water levels in Gatun Lake, the main reservoir that feeds the canal’s lock system.

World.title: Vicuña Copper Project Gets US$9.7 Billion Argentina Approval
World.content:
Argentina · Business

Key Facts —Total investment US$9.737 billion initial commitment, potentially scaling to US$18 billion over a decade. —Joint venture Vicuña Argentina S.A. is a 50/50 partnership between global miners BHP and Lundin Mining. —Location The project develops the Josemaría and Filo del Sol copper-gold-silver deposits in San Juan province. —RIGI benefits Grants 30 years of tax, customs, and foreign-exchange stability under Argentina’s large-investment regime. —Job creation Expected to generate more than 31,000 direct and indirect jobs during construction and operation.

Argentina’s national government has formally approved the Vicuna copper project under its flagship incentive regime for large investments, locking in a US$9.737 billion (9,737 million) initial commitment that stands as the largest mining investment in the country’s history. The Economy Ministry’s Resolution 1154/2026, issued in July 2026, classifies the BHP and Lundin Mining joint venture as a Strategic Long-Term Export Project, or PEELP, granting it three decades of legal and tax stability.

Vicuña Copper Project Gets US$9.7B RIGI Nod. (Photo internet reproduction)

What the RIGI Regime Actually Grants

For foreign investors unfamiliar with Argentina’s volatile regulatory history, the RIGI (Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones) is President Javier Milei’s central tool to attract capital. It applies to projects exceeding US$200 million and aims to create a predictable island of rules that cannot be changed unilaterally by future governments.

Under the PEELP classification, the Vicuña copper project secures a fixed 25% corporate income tax rate. It also locks in zero export duties after the first three years of production and eliminates import tariffs on capital goods and supplies.

Crucially, the regime guarantees free availability of foreign currency. The company can retain export proceeds abroad and is not forced to liquidate dollars into the local peso market at the official rate, which currently hovers near 1,320 pesos per US dollar. This removes a major risk that has historically deterred hard-rock mining investment in Argentina.

Scale of the San Juan Investment

The initial US$9.737 billion commitment is just the first phase. Regulatory filings indicate the total capital expenditure could scale to roughly US$18 billion over a decade as the project moves from construction into full-scale extraction and processing. The company is obligated to deploy a minimum of US$2.009 billion within the first two years.

The Vicuña district straddles the high Andes in San Juan province, a jurisdiction that has actively courted miners while other Argentine provinces have restricted activity. The project consolidates the development of the Josemaría and Filo del Sol deposits, which hold significant copper, gold, and silver resources.

Once operational, the project is projected to generate annual exports worth roughly US$2,600 million. This single mining complex would therefore make a material impact on Argentina’s trade balance, which has been under severe pressure due to the country’s chronic shortage of US dollars.

The BHP-Lundin Partnership

Vicuña Argentina S.A. is the local entity controlled equally by Australia’s BHP and Canada’s Lundin Mining. The two global firms formed the joint venture to combine their adjacent landholdings and share the massive infrastructure costs required to mine at altitudes above 4,000 meters.

BHP, the world’s largest mining company, brings deep capital reserves and experience in operating giant copper mines in Chile. Lundin Mining has a long operational history in the Americas. Their partnership signals to the market that Argentina’s regulatory framework, under RIGI, now meets the threshold required for institutional-grade mining investment.

The approval is the 22nd project to enter the RIGI framework since its creation. However, no previous approval comes close to the financial scale of Vicuña, making it the definitive test case for whether the Milei administration’s incentive package can deliver a mega-project on time and on budget.

Why Copper Matters Now

Global copper demand is projected to double by 2035, driven by electrification, renewable energy infrastructure, and electric vehicles. Existing mines are aging and grades are declining, creating a structural supply deficit that has pushed major miners to seek new frontiers.

Argentina sits on a stretch of the same Andean copper belt that has made Chile the world’s top producer. Yet Argentina has never brought a world-class copper mine into production. The Vicuña copper project is designed to change that, potentially positioning San Juan as a globally significant copper district.

For expatriates and investors living in Argentina or watching from abroad, the project’s approval under RIGI represents a real-time stress test. If the legal guarantees hold and infrastructure is built, it could unlock a pipeline of other stalled copper projects in the region.

Economic and Political Context

The approval comes as the Milei government seeks to anchor investor confidence through concrete milestones rather than rhetoric. The RIGI regime was passed as part of a broader emergency economic package and is designed to bypass provincial tax instability by offering a federal umbrella of protections.

San Juan province has long been mining-friendly, but national policy swings have previously killed investor appetite. The 30-year stability granted to Vicuña means that even if a future government raises corporate taxes or imposes capital controls, the project’s original terms remain legally binding.

More than 31,000 jobs are expected to flow from the project, a significant figure for a province with a population of roughly 800,000. Local supply chains, logistics firms, and service providers in San Juan are already positioning to capture contracts during the initial two-year, US$2.009 billion deployment phase.

Risks and Next Steps

Despite the federal approval, the project must still navigate provincial permitting, water access rights, and community agreements in the high-altitude desert region. Argentine courts have historically been receptive to environmental injunctions against mining projects, though RIGI includes provisions to expedite legal challenges.

The joint venture must also finalize a definitive feasibility study that integrates the Josemaría and Filo del Sol deposits into a single mine plan. Infrastructure requirements are daunting: new roads, power lines, and possibly a dedicated processing plant must be built in remote terrain.

For foreign investors, the immediate signal is clear. Argentina has put its legal framework behind a world-class copper asset. The execution risk now shifts from the government to the companies, and the global mining industry will be watching whether BHP and Lundin can turn a regulatory victory into a producing mine.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Vicuña copper project?

It is a US$9.737 billion joint venture between BHP and Lundin Mining to develop the Josemaría and Filo del Sol copper-gold-silver deposits in San Juan province, Argentina. It is the largest mining investment in Argentine history.

What does the RIGI regime guarantee to foreign investors?

RIGI grants 30 years of tax stability, including a fixed 25% corporate income tax rate, zero export duties after year three, and free access to foreign currency without mandatory conversion to pesos. It applies to investments over US$200 million.

How many jobs will the Vicuña project create?

The project is expected to generate more than 31,000 direct and indirect jobs during construction and operation, with projected annual exports of roughly US$2,600 million once operational.

World.title: Grynspan UN Secretary-General Bid Leads First Straw Poll
World.content:
Latin America · Politics

Key Facts —Straw poll date The UN Security Council held its first informal, secret straw poll on July 30, 2026. —Grynspan’s result Rebeca Grynspan received 10 encourage votes, 1 discourage, and 4 no opinion. —Runner-up Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana placed second with 9 encourage votes. —Candidate field Seven candidates are declared; five come from Latin America and the Caribbean. —Binding status The straw poll is informal and non-binding; any permanent member can still veto.

Grynspan UN Secretary-General candidate Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica led the first informal straw poll conducted by the United Nations Security Council on July 30, 2026, placing a Latin American woman as the early front-runner to succeed António Guterres.
