World.title: Support for students
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith (right) confabs with Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange at the post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, where Johnson Smith updated the nation on the situation with Jamaican medical students in Cuba.Garfield Robinson

THE Government of Jamaica has pledged continued support for the roughly 270 Jamaican students still studying in crisis-hit Cuba, with Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith reaffirming the Government’s commitment to the students’

welfare.

Johnson Smith told a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday that her ministry has been closely monitoring the students who remain in Cuba, 40 of whom are sponsored by Cuban scholarships, which are supported by the Government of Jamaica, further noting that one private student has formally advised of his return home.

Meanwhile, she noted that more than 65 students, including five on government scholarships, have completed their medical studies for the 2025-2026 academic year.

“Three others have indicated that they are in the process of continuing their studies elsewhere through academic transfer, and we have to caveat these numbers because we understand anecdotally that others have returned, but they have not formally notified us,” Johnson Smith said.

“And this is understandable, they are there privately, and on their own steam, but just to say that we have the information…and we also have a line of communication that allows for them to not only indicate their return, but to request assistance if they so need,” said the minister.

Johnson Smith noted that those students who remain are offered pathways to repatriation should they express a desire to return.

“This is because our concern remains for their safety, well-being, and academic continuity. We know that prolonged power cuts and reduced public transportation causes challenges for their way of life, and the Government has communicated our preparedness to assist with one-way return tickets should they wish to return but have a difficulty with affordability,” she said.

“We continue to engage the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Health, as well as medical tertiary institutions on what, if anything, can be done for those who may wish to return and continue their studies here,” she added.

Many of the Cuban medical students have seen classes suspended or moved online with limited connectivity, as Cuba faces an ongoing energy crisis, worsened by a United States blockade on fuel shipments.

The island’s fuel shortages have been triggering frequent, lengthy, and unpredictable electricity interruptions, affecting not only education but also access to food, medical supplies, and transportation.

Back in February, Johnson Smith said some students had been reaching out and advised that their institutions either closed for a period, in one case for four weeks; and others said that classes had been suspended in favour of virtual studies, which saw challenges with Internet and electricity.

To maintain direct contact, Johnson Smith noted the ministry created a WhatsApp group, at that time linking roughly 320 students with officials in Kingston and the Jamaican Embassy in Havana, a move that allowed the Government to register many privately funded students who were previously outside formal channels.

In the meantime, Johnson Smith said Wednesday that the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to Cuba by contributing US$100,000 through the Caribbean Community (Caricom) as a humanitarian relief effort.

She said Jamaica joined Caricom heads of Government in continuing to express deep concern over the worsening humanitarian situation in Cuba and reaffirmed its commitment to a coordinated regional response to provide humanitarian assistance to the Cuban people.

“While speaking as long-standing friends of both the United States and Cuba, Caricom underscored in our joint single statement that civilian needs must remain the highest priority. We welcomed recent rounds of discussions between the governments and continue to advocate for constructive dialogue as the most effective path to relieve hardship on the people of Cuba,” said Johnson Smith.

The minister added that many Cuban medical professionals who had left the island following an abrupt end to the long-standing health technical cooperation arrangement in March 2026 have since returned to Jamaica and are continuing work under new arrangements with the health and wellness ministry. Johnson Smith added that those who chose to remain are still being accommodated as they continue to work under individual contracts.

“We all continue to value the significant contribution that Cuban medical professionals have made to our health sector over many years, and following the conclusion of the technical cooperation programme, you’d recall that a number of Cuban medical professionals chose to remain in Jamaica and continue to work under personal contracts,” she said.

“Others who had left have since returned and, again, are working here under individual contracts. So we just want to confirm that, under the new arrangements, the Ministry of Health and Wellness engages Cuban professionals on an individual basis in keeping

World.title: France ups Spanish border checks as Schengen unity wobbles over Ceuta crisis
World.content:
Nuñez’s office did not immediately provide additional details on where the increased controls would take place.

France is part of the Schengen area but has repeatedly renewed its authorization to proceed with temporary internal border checks since the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks, using provisions in the Schengen Borders Code that allow such measures in response to serious security threats.

But the images of people pouring into Ceuta, an autonomous city of about 80,000 people and one of the European Union’s only two land borders with Africa, have drawn scrutiny far beyond Paris — especially among right-wing and far-right parties across Europe who seized on the incident to call for heightened restrictions on migration.

“The images coming from Ceuta are shocking and demonstrate, once again, that uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a real threat to the security of Europe’s borders,” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X.

Javí Lopez, the vice-president of the European Parliament and a member of the Socialists and Democrats, called Meloni’s comments “unworthy of a European partner.”

“After 700,000+ arrivals from Libya, Italy received European support, not lectures. Solidarity is not a one-way street,” Lopez said.

World.title: Sánchez sends armed forces to Ceuta amid migration chaos
World.content:
Videos circulating on social media showed hundreds of migrants either breaking through border gates or swimming from Morocco to the Spanish enclave on Thursday. At least 19 people died while attempting to reach Spain, police told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.

Munaim, a Moroccan athlete who once represented Morocco on the international stage as a beach football player, was among the tens of thousands of people who crossed into Ceuta on Thursday.

“I came to Ceuta because, ever since I was a child, I wanted to go to Spain,” Munaim told The Telegraph, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. “I hope to become a professional footballer in Spain,” he added.

“There were so many people during the crossing – children, adults, women and men,” he recalls — but despite the danger, Munaim insists he never considered turning back.

Behind the decision, he says, lies the hope of giving his family opportunities he believes he cannot find at home: “I’m doing this for my family. All I ask is that they keep me in their prayers.”

For Sánchez’s left-wing government, the crisis could become a diplomatic nightmare. Italy’s right-wing leader Giorgia Meloni has called for the suspension of the Schengen agreement, or for Spain to be kicked out of the free-travel zone. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on X on Friday that France would set up controls at the country’s border with Spain.

World.title: Die Angezählte
World.content:
Dafür hätten sie auch bereitwillig bis in die Abendstunden beisammen gesessen, berichten die Azubis, freiwillig Überstunden gemacht. „Und Sie leben noch“, ruft ihnen Reiche mit einem Lachen zu. „Je näher man Berlin kommt, desto mehr nimmt der Glaube daran ab, dass das geht.“

Umstrittene Persönlichkeit

Es sind genau diese Aussagen, die Reiche zu einer umstrittenen Politikerin gemacht haben. Vielleicht noch mehr als ihre konkreten Gesetzesvorhaben. Die einen feiern sie für ihre Direktheit, sehen in ihr eine Ordoliberale, die nach dem Grünen Robert Habeck im Wirtschaftsministerium aufräumt und endlich vieles ausspricht, was zuletzt keinen politischen Raum hatte. Andere werfen Reiche vor, sich vor allem bei Themen aus der Deckung zu wagen, die nicht in ihr Ressort gehören, etwa bei Rentenfragen.

Und dann gibt es noch den Dauervorwurf: Schlechte Personalführung. Sie gilt als fordernde Chefin, die Stimmung im Haus als angespannt bis unterkühlt. Frühere Wegbegleiter berichten dasselbe aus ihrer Zeit als Chefin von Westenergie.

Connemann ist ein Verlust

Auch mit Connemann war Reiche nicht besonders eng. Dennoch schwächt ihr Abgang das Haus. Mit Connemann hatte Reiche die einflussreiche MIT-Chefin der Union an ihrer Seite, die ihr automatisch mehr Gewicht verlieh.

Als Connemann vom Kanzler gefragt wurde, ob sie ins Digitalministerium wechseln wolle, habe sie auf der Stelle zugesagt. Einzige Bedingung sei gewesen, den Titel der Mittelstandsbeauftragten mitzunehmen, der traditionell im Wirtschaftsministerium angesiedelt ist.

Daran hänge kein Personal, keine Förderung, heißt es aus dem Haus. Allerdings fiel Reiche bisher nicht für ihren starken Einsatz für den Mittelstand auf. Damit hinterlässt Connemann eine Lücke.

World.title: Week Ender — Searing Contradiction: Wildfires and climate politics
World.content:
Wildfires may sound remote — something that happens deep in a forest or on an empty mountainside. But in Europe, there’s often very little distance between nature and major population centers. That’s why the fires near Bordeaux and Madrid have been so frightening: they’re not burning somewhere far away, but threatening homes, businesses and entire urban regions.

European countries are responding by sending planes, helicopters and hundreds of firefighters to help one another. But while Europe has built an effective system for reacting once the flames are raging, it’s still struggling with the less dramatic work of prevention.

POLITICO senior climate reporter Zia Weise joins host Sarah Wheaton, sustainability reporter Marianne Gros and Agnes Rønberg from the agriculture team to examine how abandoned land, poorly managed forests and disappearing livestock are making fires harder to control.

They also unpack the growing bill for homes, farms and businesses — and how the costs eventually spread to insurers and cash-strapped governments — while asking whether Brussels can prepare Europe for worsening climate disasters as it rolls back parts of the Green Deal.

World.title: Football and politics, brought to you by Big Business (and energy drinks)
World.content:
In “United Passions” — which really should have been called “Balls” — Blatter is played by Tim Roth, a fine actor who admitted he took the role to pay for his kids to go to college. If the movie was, heaven help us, ever updated to include Infantino’s tenure, surely the role would go to either Stanley Tucci or the ghost of late Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin.

Infantino has, you will doubtless be aware, decided to sell football off to the highest bidder, with FIFA publishing a proposal that would privatize the World Cup’s commercial operations. A venture capital firm headed by Josh Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is lined up as the lead investor in the proposed deal. Of course it is. The scheme is known as FIFA Forward Enterprise or FFE — although FFS seems rather more appropriate.

I, for one, am looking forward to the Raytheon World Cup of 2038 in South Sudan, where the 18-karat gold trophy depicting two human figures holding up the Earth is replaced by a cheap plastic bobblehead of Trump with his pants around his ankles.

But not everyone is so keen on Infantino’s plan. Glenn Micallef, the EU’s sports commissioner, pointed out that football “isn’t baseball,” which is very perceptive of him. It’s also not cross-country skiing, knitting or a cauliflower.

Micallef’s point is, of course, that football hasn’t — and shouldn’t — reach the level of commercialization of American sports, although it had a damn good go during this summer’s World Cup with the introduction of hydration breaks sponsored by Powerade.

But the further monetization of sports feels inevitable; it is entertainment, after all. Will politics go the same way? When, for example, will we see EU summits sponsored by Red Bull, the European Commission midday briefing brought to you by Xanax, or Germany sponsored by sausages in a glass jar?

World.title: Why Andy Burnham is no ordinary Labour prime minister
World.content:
The Labour Party and the Co-operative Party are distinct organizations — but a pact agreed in 1927 allows candidates to stand on behalf of both parties.

In practice, Co-operative MPs tend to follow the Labour line — but the party has a distinct focus on mutual ownership, community businesses, and credit unions. It argues for democratic control of services and businesses by the people who use them — and supporters say this program offers up real hints about how Burnham will now govern.

Since returning to the Westminster frontline, the new prime minister has hardly been shy about his administration’s support for the co-operative drive.

“If people, in 1844, could form the co-operative movement in Rochdale to lower the price of food, then why can’t we act now, with similar courage, to make life better?” he asked in his first major speech after winning the Makerfield by-election. That was a direct callback to a group of working-class weavers — known as the Rochdale Pioneers — credited with founding the modern cooperative movement by pooling wages to set up a worker-owned store at a time of soaring food costs.

The Co-operative Party was “created for a slightly different purpose” to Labour, says International Development Minister Kirsty McNeill — a Labour and Co-operative MP like Burnham, It is about getting a better deal “as a consumer in the marketplace and where you live.”

“It’s going to be a moment of unprecedented opportunity for the co-operative movement,” says Caitlin Prowle, the party’s assistant general secretary. “I believe that this new team is very serious about rewiring our economy, rewiring society and shifting power.”

World.title: Russia’s Olympic win comes with a price for Putin
World.content:
But while Russia has been trumpeting its big diplomatic win, and the IOC has drawn international ire for its decision, what Moscow quietly agreed to in order to achieve its victory garnered far less attention — a quiet renunciation of what Moscow claims as “sovereign territory.”

What lies behind the IOC’s reversal was confirmation that the Russian Olympic Committee “no longer includes as its members any regional sports organisations in territories falling under the jurisdiction of the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine” — that means Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

A woman holds a sign with the text “Boycott Russian sport at the Olympics” during a march in memory of the hundreds of Ukrainian athletes killed since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in Paris on July 13, 2024. | Remon Haazen/Getty Images

These four territories of great economic, industrial and historic importance for President Putin have been a major sticking point in ending the war since Russia annexed them in 2022 in defiance of international law. And this concession made on the global stage is now turning into a domestic political scandal, drawing criticism from the country’s influential pro-war commentators who see it as a betrayal of the Kremlin’s territorial claims.

“The Russian Olympic Committee gave up part of the country’s territory just to live it up in style at the Olympics,” wrote famous pro-war journalist Dmitry Steshin — just one of many discontented voices.

‘Sabotage at a state level’

This is not the first clash between the Kremlin’s international sports ambitions and its influential military bloggers.

Russia’s attempts to send its athletes to the 2024 Olympics under neutral status — a restriction imposed by the IOC after 2023 — had similarly triggered widespread backlash, with the country’s pro-war commentators accusing authorities of “betraying national interests.”

World.title: How Greece’s ‘door visa’ gives Turkish visitors easier entry to islands in the EU
World.content:
A visa-on-arrival scheme for Turkish travellers to visit 12 Greek islands has greatly simplified access to this corner of the EU, which was previously off-limits without a hard-to-get Schengen visa.

 

Introduced in April 2024, the scheme, known in Türkiye as the "door visa" (kapi vizesi), initially covered 10 Greek islands before being renewed and expanded to 12 last year.

The list of islands in the Aegean Sea – all near the Turkish coast – includes Chios, Kalymnos, Kastellorizo, Kos, Leros, Lesvos, Limnos, Patmos, Rhodes, Samos, Samothraki and Symi.

It allows Turkish citizens to visit participating islands for up to seven days without obtaining a full Schengen visa in advance, but cannot be extended and does not permit onward travel to mainland Greece or to other Schengen-area countries.

"Getting a Schengen visa is becoming increasingly difficult for Turks, but this new system makes it easy and fast for us to visit the Greek islands," Emirhan Gurses, a 21-year-old student from Manisa, told AFP.

Nearly 1.5 million Turks visited the country in 2025, up from 1.2 million in 2024, according to Bank of Greece figures. Turkish travel agents say most of them took advantage of the express visa to see the islands.

For many Turks, it has offered an affordable alternative at a time when soaring inflation has made holidays at home increasingly expensive.

During a visit to Ankara in February, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis hailed the scheme as "particularly successful".

"In the last year alone, hundreds of thousands of Turkish friends have travelled to the Greek islands, bringing our peoples closer together," Mitsotakis said, adding that both countries want to renew the programme.

‘Perfect place to start’

For Ikra Altumsek, and many other Turkish tourists, the scheme has offered the chance to visit some of Greece’s most popular island destinations.

"I think Samos was the perfect place to start," the 21-year-old university student said, wheeling her luggage alongside her mother as they waited for a ferry off the Greek island of Samos.

They were heading back to Kusadasi, on Türkiye's Aegean coast after a sun-drenched vacation – Altumsek's first trip abroad.

With its turquoise waters, quiet coves, traditional villages and waterfront restaurants, Samos – situated just opposite the Turkish coast – combines beaches and natural beauty with a rich cultural heritage, including ancient sites linked to Pythagoras, one of the most famous figures of the ancient Greek world.

Turkish-flagged boats carrying tourists are a constant presence along the waterfront, arriving and departing throughout the day, highlighting the steady flow of Turkish visitors to the Greek island.

"Τhe food is delicious. I have a 17-year-old son, and he keeps asking me, 'Mum, when are we going to Greece to eat?'," said Nevin Cagliguney, 51.

The crowds arriving on Samos reflect the diversity of society in Türkiye, which is not part of the EU but has ambitions to one day join it.

Among the visitors are young travellers discovering the island for the first time, as well as families including women wearing headscarves, accompanied by their spouses and children in strollers.

Many restaurants display Turkish-language menus outside their entrances.

A ‘big difference’ to the economy

The visa-on-arrival scheme comes as Turkish demand for travel to the EU has outpaced the capacity of many consulates to process Schengen visa applications, leaving applicants facing long waits, rising costs and uncertainty over approvals.

For tour guide Mikail Esabalioglu, a Greek resident of Samos originally from Istanbul, Turkish visitors have become an increasingly important part of the island's tourism economy.

"We receive many Turkish guests, especially from Izmir and other parts of Türkiye's Aegean coast," he said.

But the programme could be improved even further, he said "because visitors sometimes have to wait a long time at the entrance and the arrival process can be difficult".

Samos business owner Giannis Kagias said Turkish visitors had "made a big difference" to the island's economy.

"Our Turkish friends who come here are a great support," he said. "Without Turkish visitors, I think the situation for businesses on the island would be much more difficult."

Selim Zuberi, a 38-year-old consultant from Mersin, said the programme was also important for bringing people from the two neighbouring countries closer.

People can "experience each other's cultures", he said. "History has had its conflicts, but we should not carry those burdens forever. We should enjoy life".

World.title: Eurozone inflation hits 2.9%: Which countries saw the biggest increases?
World.content:
Europe's inflation slowdown proved short-lived.

 

After easing in June, consumer price growth in the eurozone accelerated again in July as the renewed conflict in the Middle East drove energy costs higher.

Eurostat's flash estimate showed that annual consumer price inflation across the bloc rose to 2.9% in July, up from 2.8% in June and in line with economists' expectations.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, also ticked higher to 2.5%, from 2.4%. Energy recorded the highest annual jump, with prices rising 10% year-on-year, followed by services, up 3.3%.

That comes just one day after eurozone GDP unexpectedly accelerated in the second quarter, reinforcing the view that Europe's economy remains far more resilient than many had feared.

But beneath the headline, inflation trends varied sharply across the eurozone, with some countries seeing price pressures intensify while others experienced a notable slowdown.

Lithuania remained an inflation hotspot

Lithuania recorded the highest inflation rate in the eurozone in July at 5.6%, followed by Bulgaria (4.1%), Cyprus (4.0%), Spain (3.8%) and Croatia (3.6%).

At the opposite end of the spectrum, Estonia reported the lowest annual inflation rate at 2.0%, ahead of Malta (2.1%), France (2.4%), Latvia (2.5%), Austria (2.6%) and Finland (2.6%).

Germany, the bloc's largest economy, saw inflation accelerate to 2.8%, while Italy matched the eurozone average at 2.9%.

"We think headline inflation will remain sticky at just above 2.5% for the Eurozone," Pantheon Economics' economist Claus Vistesen commented on the data.

The firm expects the European Central Bank to deliver another 25-basis-point rate hike before pausing.

Where inflation accelerated and where it eased

Compared with June, inflationary pressures evolved in very different directions across the bloc.

The sharpest monthly increase was recorded in the Netherlands, where consumer prices rose 1.5% from June, followed by Germany (+0.9%), France (+0.6%), Croatia (+0.6%), Malta (+0.6%), Estonia (+0.5%) and Bulgaria (+0.4%).

By contrast, prices fell most sharply in Greece (-1.4%), followed by Italy (-1.0%), Latvia (-0.7%), Belgium (-0.6%), Luxembourg (-0.6%), Austria (-0.4%), Portugal (-0.3%) and Slovenia (-0.3%).

"The ongoing conflict and a spike in energy costs remain key risks to growth, given that the Eurozone is a net importer of energy," said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at global financial services firm Ebury.

"While oil prices have eased from their highs, they remain elevated, and the rise in natural gas prices to multi-year highs is adding to concerns," he added.

Markets remain in "risk-on" mode

Risk appetite remained strong across markets following Wall Street's powerful rally the previous session, when Microsoft surged 15% after blowout quarterly earnings, marking its strongest single-day gain since 2008.

The euro strengthened modestly against the US dollar to 1.1520 immediately after the inflation figures, while European equities extended Thursday's rally.

Germany's DAX 40 climbed about 0.8% to a fresh record high above 25,800, the Euro Stoxx 50 gained more than 1% to an all-time high, France's CAC 40 advanced around 0.9%, and Italy's FTSE MIB outperformed with a gain approaching 1%.

Technology shares again led the advance.

Infineon Technologies jumped more than 6%, extending the AI-driven rebound across global semiconductor stocks. STMicroelectronics gained more than 4%, while Siemens Energy climbed around 3.5%.

Corporate earnings continued to reinforce sentiment.

Saint-Gobain rallied after reporting stronger second-quarter sales growth. NatWest advanced following a 29% jump in pre-tax profit, while Engie and Crédit Agricole also traded higher after better-than-expected results.

World.title: Raffaele Fitto in Nicosia: EU seeks key role in Cyprus talks
World.content:
Raffaele Fitto underlined the European Union's intention to take on a significant role in the UN process on the Cyprus issue, following his meeting with the President of the Republic of Cyprus, Nikos Christodoulides, in Nicosia.

 

The European Commission's special representative for Cyprus and Executive Vice-President of the Commission was received on Friday morning at the Presidential Palace, during his first visit to the island since his appointment.

"The European Union is sending a very clear message: that it wishes to work and to take part with a very significant role in the United Nations process," Raffaele Fitto said after the meeting.

Raffaele Fitto and Nikos Christodoulides Stavros Ioannides/PIO

He stressed that it is important for the EU "to contribute positively to the process", noting that the purpose of his first visit is to listen to the positions of the parties involved.

Fitto announced that he will return to Cyprus in the coming months and expressed the view that over the same period "very significant results" could be achieved.

“We want to follow the UN process clearly, because it is very important for us to make a significant and positive contribution in this way,” he said.

Next steps discussed

Cyprus's Foreign Minister, Constantinos Kombos, described the meeting as "particularly useful and constructive", explaining that the next steps were discussed both at a practical level and in terms of the contacts Mr Fitto will have with the parties involved.

Constantinos Kombos and Raffaele Fitto Stavros Ioannides/PIO

"We view his visit to Cyprus extremely positively. The timing is also very important, given that only a few days ago we had the Secretary-General here," he said.

According to the Cypriot foreign minister, Nicosia believes that European Union–Turkey relations can be used to give fresh momentum to efforts to reach a settlement.

"EU–Turkey relations are an issue that can serve as leverage," he said, adding that the appointment of an Executive Vice-President of the European Commission carries particular weight, as Fitto already has channels of communication with Turkey.

Mr Kombos also said that the Cypriot side has "thoughts, ideas and proposals" that are currently under discussion, as well as new proposals for a possible acceleration of the process before António Guterres's term ends in December.

"There is potential for progress. We are working to create the conditions for that progress. But the answer to all these questions lies in Ankara," he underlined.

Meeting with Erhürman

After his meeting with Nikos Christodoulides, Raffaele Fitto is expected to hold a separate meeting with Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhürman.

The visit is taking place just days after UN Secretary-General António Guterres's contacts in Cyprus and his intention to convene a new, broader meeting, provided sufficient preparation is carried out beforehand.

According to the European Commission, Fitto's mission is to assist the settlement process under UN auspices, in close cooperation with the Secretary-General's personal envoy, María Ángela Holguín, and in contact with both sides and the other parties involved.

The Commission has declared itself ready to play an "active role" with the instruments and tools at its disposal, reiterating its support for a solution based on a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation, in line with UN Security Council resolutions and the European acquis.

World.title: Danube drought exposes everything from shipwrecks to centuries-old projectiles
World.content:
Budapest's Danube River level dropped to record lows this week, reaching 23 centimetres on Wednesday (29 July). The previous lowest water level, 33 centimetres, was recorded in 2018.

 

By Wednesday lunchtime the water level had risen slightly, to 25 centimetres, but no significant improvement is expected. What is more, the summer’s second major heatwave is just now reaching Hungary.

As the Danube recedes, more and more of the riverbed is being exposed. The situation is so extraordinary that the president of the Hungarian Cyclists’ Club, Gábor Dezső Kürti, was able to cycle along the riverbed all the way from Budapest to Vác. A few days ago, a Euronews reader came across a strange, perfectly shaped stone on the riverbed near Visegrád, which immediately caught his attention.

Mysterious stone sphere in the Danube olvasónktól

Danube drought exposes everything from shipwrecks to centuries-old projectiles

The reader also informed the Mátyás Király Museum in Visegrád about their discovery, and on first look it appears it could be a catapult projectile.

The museum’s director, archaeologist Gergely Buzás, tells Euronews that such finds are not uncommon in the area; after all, Visegrád Castle was bombarded with hundreds of stone balls during each siege, so they also have a few similar projectiles in their storeroom.

The museum’s experts will go out next week to examine the stone sphere to confirm their prediction.

How old it is can only be guessed at, not measured. According to Buzás, what can at least be said is that such projectiles were used up to the 16th century at the latest. But it could go back much further, since a fort already stood here in Roman times and stone-throwing machines were already known then.

So if it is confirmed that this really is a catapult projectile, it was made at least 400, and possibly as much as 2,000 years ago, and has been lying on the bed of the Danube ever since.

Discoveries of this kind are not isolated now: last week a Second World War shipwreck also emerged from the drying bed of the Danube near Mohács.

No end to the drought in sight

From the area where the mysterious stone sphere was found, the Danube Bend, the European Union’s Copernicus satellite earth observation programme published a satellite image on Wednesday. The montage shows the same stretch of the Danube in an image from 14 July 2025 and another from 25 July 2026.

Huge difference compared with last year Európai Unió, Copernicus Sentinel-2 műholdfelvétel

Comparing the two images, it is clear that this year there is much less water in the Danube than there was last July. Sandbanks have emerged on the river’s bends, making navigation on the Danube extremely difficult. It is no coincidence that on some stretches neither cargo nor passenger vessels can operate, and restrictions on river traffic have also been introduced in Budapest.

The head of the Ministry Responsible for the Living Environment, László Gajdos, declared a state of heightened alert in the fight against drought on Wednesday. In the morning the minister announced that "in 66 of the country’s 84 water-shortage management districts, the drought index is above the triple threshold value laid down in law", meaning that three quarters of the country are suffering severe water shortages.

The drought situation on HungaroMet’s map HungaroMet

According to the weather forecasts, there will be no rain at all over the next two weeks. The heatwave that began on Wednesday is expected to reach its peak in about a week, with maximum temperatures of around 39 degrees in the capital. Some relief is expected only towards the end of next week, and even then maximums of 31–33 degrees are still to be expected.

This isn't just a run of bad luck with the weather. According to a World Weather Attribution analysis published last week, Europe's droughts this year have been driven less by a shortage of rain and more by extreme heat, which pulls moisture out of rivers, soil and vegetation far faster than usual. Scientists found such intensely evaporative conditions are now up to 80 times more likely than before humans started heating the planet with fossil fuels.

World.title: Behind Europe’s mega fires: Would France and Spain still be ablaze if it weren’t for climate change?
World.content:
Human-induced climate change made the fire-prone conditions that have devastated large swathes of Europe up to 20 times more likely, scientists have warned.

 

Spain and France have been grappling with uncontained blazes that have scorched more than 120,000 hectares of land and forced around 300,000 people to evacuate their homes. The EU activated its emergency response system, sending firefighting aircraft and ground vehicles to tackle the blazes – but warned it was quickly running “out of capacity”.

Earlier this week, a wildfire in France grew so powerful that its own smoke column turned into a thunderstorm, generating lightning that struck the ground and ignited even more fires. It also produced heavy winds that pushed the flames in new directions.

More recently, wildfires have broken out in Greece – killing three firefighters on the island of Crete – while hundreds have been evacuated along Türkiye’s western and southern coasts.

While the blazes have garnered global media attention, many outlets have avoided linking Europe’s so-called ‘mega fires’ to climate change.

Has climate change increased the likelihood of Europe’s mega fires?

A new study from World Weather Attribution (WWA) analysed historical weather observations – but not climate models – to see how fire-prone weather conditions have changed over time.

To do this, they used a metric called the Daily Severity Rating (DSR), which incorporates hot, dry, and windy conditions and reflects how difficult a fire is to suppress once it has started. The researchers looked at the seven-day period with the highest DSR across southwestern France and central Spain, where the fires occurred.

They found that human-induced climate change made the fire-prone conditions at least twice as likely in southwestern France and at least 20 times as likely in central Spain. The scientists note that these are conservative estimates.

“When wildfires break out simultaneously across different regions, it becomes clear that human-induced climate change is not only increasing the likelihood of more extreme fires but also their synchronicity,” says Andreia Ribeiro, a climate scientist at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research in Germany.

“That comes with a real cost, as overlapping fire extremes make it harder for countries to cooperate and share firefighting resources with each other when that support is needed most.”

The analysis found that in today’s climate, events of this intensity are expected to occur once every 20 years in southwestern France and once every six years in central Spain.

Dr Clair Barnes, a research associate in extreme weather and climate change at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London, says the wildfires aren’t just a case of “bad luck” and are a “clear sign on the escalating impacts of anthropogenic warming”.

“A wet winter, followed by this intensely dry summer and a succession of heatwaves has left forests loaded with dry fuel, and relentless heat – fuelled by human-caused climate change – has created the conditions for sparks to take hold and become massive, dangerous wildfires,” she says.

Yesterday (30 July), a separate study published in the journal Scientific Reports analysed national wildfire records from Portugal, Spain, France, Italy and Greece alongside weather and climate data between 1981 and 2025.

Researchers found that in parts of France and Spain, the intensity of fire-promoting weather had increased by up to 50 per cent between 2016 and 2025 compared with 1981 to 2010.

The number of days with “highly fire-promoting conditions” also increased from fewer than 10 days per summer in 1981 to 2010 to around 25 days over the last decade in parts of each country studied.

UN urges Europe to move from fossil fuels ‘faster’

Following WWA’s attribution analysis, UN climate change Executive Secretary Simon Steill says Europe’s mega fires show how fast climate change-driven extreme heat and dry landscapes can turn wildfires into “devastating national disasters”.

“Humanity continuing to burn colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas is baking our planet, making these conditions more dangerous, and these mega fires more deadly and destructive,” he says.

“But the solutions are equally clear: all countries must move faster from fossil fuels to renewables and protect people from worsening climate impacts, from wildfires, to megastorms and floods, to droughts hitting food production.”

According to the European Commission, the number of people living near wildland and exposed to high-to-extreme fire danger levels for at least 10 days per year in the EU would grow by 15 million with just 3°C of warming. Human-caused climate change has already pushed the global surface temperature up by approximately 1.3-1.5℃ compared to pre-industrial levels.

World.title: Farewell Franco Baresi: Milan mourns an icon, world football loses a legend
World.content:
Italian football is paying tribute to one of its greatest icons, Franco Baresi, the legendary captain of AC Milan and the Italian national team, who has died at the age of 66.

 

Widely regarded as one of the finest defenders of all time, the news was announced on Thursday morning by the Rossoneri club in a message posted on its official channels.

"The entire history of AC Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi. His example and integrity will be forever etched into the Club's DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is. The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi's family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own."

His death symbolically closes an era for Milan and for Italian football, which has lost one of its most iconic leading figures.

AC Milan statement on the death of their legendary captain Franco Baresi

A one-club man

Born on 8 May 1960 in Travagliato, in the province of Brescia, Baresi began his football journey as Milan's youth academy. He made his Serie A debut in 1978, aged just 17, and went on to build a career that would bind him forever to the Rossoneri red and black colours.

In twenty years with Milan he experienced all the highs and lows of the club's recent history: from the star scudetto won in 1979 to the difficult years in Serie B, through to the return to the topof European football with Arrigo Sacchi's team and, later, with the side coached by Fabio Capello, which enjoyed a remarkable 58-game unbeaten run.

A quiet but charismatic leader, he became the face of the all-conquering Milan of the 1980s and 1990s which won several domestic and European titles.

Throughout those times, Baresi always wore the captain's armband and the number 6 shirt. He played more than 700 official matches before retiring at the end of the 1996-1997 season.

As a mark of gratitude, Milan has announced it is retiring his number 6 shirt permanently, an honour reserved for the greatest figures in the club's history.

Success with Milan and with the national team

Franco Baresi's trophy haul tells the story of an extraordinary career. With Milan he won 6 scudetti, 3 European Cups/Champions Leagues, 2 Intercontinental Cups, 2 UEFA Super Cups, 4 Italian Super Cups, 2 Serie B championships and 1 Mitropa Cup.

He also wrote important chapters in the history of Italian football with the national team. Called up by Enzo Bearzot for the 1982 World Cup, he was part of the squad that became world champions in Spain, even though he did not play.

In the following years he became a mainstay of Italy, taking third place at Italia '90 and captaining the Azzurri all the way to the final of the 1994 World Cup in the United States. In that tournament, after suffering a serious meniscus injury during the competition, he managed to recover in time for the final against Brazil, delivering a performance of the highest level before the side was defeated on penalties.

He remains the only Italian footballer to have ended his World Cup career with a first, a second and a third place finish.

Illness and the worsening of his condition

In 2025 Milan announced that routine tests had revealed a lung nodule. Baresi underwent a minimally invasive surgical procedure to remove the lesion, which was completed without complications, followed by consolidating immunotherapy.

In the months that followed he spent his convalescence away from the club's official commitments, reassuring fans with a message in which he explained that he needed time to recover.

FILE: A hatted Franco Baresi in the stands before the Serie A match between Milan and Hellas Verona, in Milan, Italy, Sunday 28 December 2025 AP Photo

In recent days unfounded reports of his death had circulated on social media. These were denied by Milan, which had nevertheless confirmed how delicate the situation was. His condition subsequently deteriorated, leading to his death.

With the death of Franco Baresi, Milan has lost its most emblematic standard-bearer and world football one of the most elegant, intelligent and successful defenders in its history. His sporting legacy will continue to live on through the exploits that defined an entire era of Italian football.

World.title: British oil giant BP prepares to sell North Sea business
World.content:
British oil and gas giant BP said on Friday that it had launched a process to market its North Sea business for a potential sale, as it looks to focus on its “highest-value opportunities”.

 

Its North Sea portfolio off the UK coast comprises five production hubs and employs about 1,100 people, BP added in a statement.

Its North Sea portfolio off the UK coast comprises five production hubs and employs about 1,100 people, BP added in a statement.

“The UK has been our home for more than 100 years and will continue to play an important role in our future. We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day,” BP chief executive Meg O'Neill said in the statement.

She added: “The North Sea remains integral to the UK's energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company. It has world-class people, resilient assets and a proud heritage, and it is precisely these qualities that can attract an owner ready to back its next chapter."

O'Neill said BP would seek a deal that recognised the business’s “people, assets and heritage”.

The announcement came a day after new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled that he could take a more flexible approach to North Sea oil and gas production, amid concerns about the UK's energy security and volatile global energy markets.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly called on Britain to ramp up oil and gas production in the North Sea. Burnham said on Thursday that he intended to take “a pragmatic approach” to developing and using the region’s resources.

BP said it would continue to focus on operating the business safely and reliably throughout the sale process.

Why North Sea production is losing its appeal

BP's North Sea business currently employs approximately 1,100 workers, and the company has operated in the region for more than 60 years. In 2025, the business produced around 117,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day, accounting for approximately 5% of BP’s global oil and gas output.

However, the ageing basin has steadily lost some of its appeal in recent years as production has declined and the UK’s frequently changing tax regime has increased the burden on producers.

However, the basin has steadily lost some of its appeal in recent years due to declining production, higher windfall taxes and the previous Labour government’s decision not to issue new licences to explore new oil and gas fields.

Oil and gas companies have also criticised the windfall tax and broader policy uncertainty, arguing that they have discouraged investment.

The company is now choosing to focus more on its core oil and gas businesses, after scaling back its investments in renewable energy. The strategic reversal followed pressure from investors to improve returns and reduce debt.

Over the past year, BP has agreed to or completed several divestments. These include an agreement to sell a 65% controlling stake in Castrol, its lubricants business, to infrastructure investment firm Stonepeak. The deal is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approval.

In the last year, the company has already agreed to or completed a number of divestments, including the sale of Castrol, its lubricants business. This is in an attempt to further simplify its portfolio, focus investment on core upstream, downstream and trading operations and bolster its balance sheet.

BP's move follows similar retreats by several other global energy companies. ExxonMobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips have sold North Sea assets, while Shell and Equinor have combined their offshore UK businesses in a joint venture. TotalEnergies has also reduced and reorganised parts of its regional portfolio as companies respond to declining production and seek more profitable projects elsewhere.

World.title: More than 40,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta over past 24 hours, Spain says
World.content:
Around 40,000 migrants have crossed in recent days from Morocco into Spain's Ceuta enclave, a police source said on Friday, as Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was due to arrive there.

 

"There was a steady stream of people all night long," a police source said, adding that migrants "continued to arrive overnight and are still arriving" early Friday.

Spanish authorities said they would try to expel those who had entered illegally as quickly as possible, despite a ​court ruling that has put some new restrictions on special "border rejection" rules that allow immediate expulsions.

It was not immediately clear whether that is what prompted the recent surge of migrants from Morocco.

Migrants return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Friday, 31 July 2026. The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Ebullient migrants on Thursday were walking through the streets of Ceuta, thanking the Spanish police and calling out: "Bye bye Morocco, hello Spain."

Police and Civil Guards in Ceuta appeared to do little to intervene, although some officers attempted to direct the arrivals to the local migrant reception centre.

Diplomatic fallout

Already, the Ceuta scenes of the surge in migrants were causing diplomatic fallout.

Italy on Thursday called for Spain to be suspended from Europe's open-borders Schengen zone, prompting Spain to summon Italy's ambassador and accuse Rome of using the crisis for political gain.

Two top officials within US President Donald Trump's White House on Thursday also reiterated their anti-immigration politics using video of Ceuta.

Hundreds of migrants who have irregularly entered Ceuta began to return to Morocco through the same chokepoint, the breakwater that separates the autonomous city. The migrants are being led by the military to find a way to return.

France reinforces border controls with Spain

The French Interior Minister, Laurent Nuñez, stated this Friday that controls on the border with Spain will be reinforced.

"In light of the situation in the enclave of Ceuta, I gave instructions yesterday evening to immediately step up controls at the Spanish border. Furthermore, I am mobilising the Rapid Border Intervention Force to carry out thorough checks," says the French Interior Minister.

Spanish authorities "overwhelmed"

Spanish authorities said they have been "completely overwhelmed" by the situation, El Mundo reports. Only 55 agents were on the front line when the situation broke out, according to the Spanish newspaper.

The active troops on the ground are "three or four times less than what would be needed to face something like this," says to El Mundo David Gomez, secretary of communication of the Justice Professional Association for the Civil Guard.

The influx marks the largest arrival of migrants in Ceuta since 2021 — predominantly young men and adolescents — with 18 deaths reported during the crossing, according to figures released on Friday morning by the same source.

The number of entries means the population of the enclave increased by around 50%, as around 83,000 people are living in Ceuta.

World.title: Indonesia: Pilot faces death penalty after drugs found in suitcase
World.content:
A Malaysian Airlines pilot tested positive for cocaine and meth after flying a passenger jet into Jakarta, with Indonesian authorities finding over 70,000 ecstasy pills in his suitcase.

A Malaysian pilot could face the death penalty in Indonesia after being arrested at Soekarno-Hatta international airport in Jakarta with more than 70,000 ecstasy pills in his luggage, Indonesian police said on Friday.

The 39-year-old, identified only as MS, was apprehended shortly after flying a ​passenger plane from Kuala Lumpur to Jakarta late on Wednesday. While the airport officials did not name the pilot's employer, the flight number indicates it was a Malaysia Airlines flight.

Customs officials said they found 14 bags of ecstasy tablets in the pilot's suitcase, plus four grams of meth in his hand luggage.

They said the pilot had transported the illicit substances at the request ​an unidentified person with the promise of a 50,000 ringgit ($12,240, €10,630) reward.

They also said the pilot had been under the influence of drugs while flying the jet.

"The results of his urine test came back positive for meth, MDMA and cocaine," said an official.

"What concerns all of us is that this person's profession is a pilot. At the time he arrived, he had just flown that plane from Kuala Lumpur to Indonesia."

Malaysia Airlines has declined ​to comment on the case while the investigation is ongoing, but said it ​does not tolerate form of misconduct and is currently conducting its own internal review.

"Malaysia Airlines will extend its full cooperation to the relevant authorities in accordance with all applicable laws and regulations," read a statement.

Cocaine, Crime, Cartels: Can Europe fight back? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pilot could face death penalty under Indonesia anti-drug laws

An officer with Indonesia's national drugs crime unit, Awaludin Amin, described the pilot as a courier working for an international syndicate. He also said this was not the first time that MS had smuggled drugs into Indonesia.

The country has some of the toughest anti-drug laws in the world. The drug-trafficking charges levied against MS can carry life sentences or even the death penalty — although the country has maintained a moratorium on executions for the last decade.

However, around 90 foreign alleged traffickers remain on death row, along with over 400 Indonesians.

Indonesia last carried out the death sentence in 2016, when one Indonesian and three Nigerians were convicted of drug offences and executed by firing squad.

In 2015, two Australian nationals were executed for attempting to smuggle heroin off the popular resort island of Bali as part of the "Bali Nine" drug ring.

In March this year, two British men were sentenced to nine and 11 years in prison respectively after being found guilty of smuggling cocaine onto Bali.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Epstein files: How victims remain exposed to identification
World.content:
US officials vowed to revise redactions after files exposed information that identified survivors of sexual abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and his associates. A DW investigation found that sensitive information remains online.

"I cannot live without looking over my shoulder," a sexual abuse survivor told US lawmakers in May, describing how her personal information was publicly exposed in January, when the Department of Justice (DOJ) released hundreds of thousands of documents related to the financier Jeffrey Epstein. "I can only imagine the long-term impact this mistake will have on my life."

Three days after the DOJ released the largest of 12 datasets on Epstein on January 30, a department lawyer told a federal court that "human or technical error" had been among the factors that led to the publishing of personally identifying information of people who had been sexually abused by Epstein and his associates. As a result, the DOJ said it would remove, review and redact flagged documents before republishing them.

DW's investigative unit, along with its Innovation and Data teams, spent months reviewing thousands of documents released by the DOJ. In the six months since the release, DW identified dozens of files that still contained information — including names, faces and email addresses — that could be used to identify survivors, witnesses and informants, among other people.

DOJ Epstein Library

By mid-February, DW had scraped more than 800,000 files from the DOJ's Epstein Library — a challenging task with the archive constantly changing: New files were being added, others were taken down and modified files were popping up after days of absence.

But it wasn't until DW obtained an earlier set of files archived by a publicly facing data preservation project on GitHub that we realized our February collection contained more than 500,000 fewer files than the earlier archived version.

To verify the contents of the original release, DW generated a unique digital fingerprint, known as a hash, for every document. Hashes confirm that a document matches the original and hasn't been altered. By comparing these fingerprints with documents scraped from the DOJ website about two weeks later, DW could determine which files matched, as well as identify documents that had been removed from the DOJ website.

DW also found that some files had changed because the digital fingerprint was no longer the same: They had the same file name but were larger or smaller than the original. When DW reviewed this subset, we found that they represented files that had been further redacted — or information was added.

In one instance, a survivor described how Epstein had abused her for years as a minor in her testimony to lawyers. Her name was redacted throughout the transcript until the last page, when a lawyer thanked her for her testimony and said her name, and it remains unredacted as of publication.

Her exposed name was not an isolated case.

US lawmakers created strict rules on how the Epstein files should be published, such as ensuring that personally identifying information of victims be redacted to protect them from public exposure Image: picture-alliance/dpa/M. Reynolds

Deep audio analysis

To analyze audio files, including victim statements and tipoffs, DW's investigative unit collaborated with the Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology's Media Distribution and Security research group in Ilmenau, Germany. The MDS specializes in audio authenticity, manipulation and speech synthesis detection.

After removing duplicated files from the publicly facing data preservation project and DW's scrape, we were left with more than 150 audio files, which the MDS's forensic audio researchers analyzed using state-of-the-art tools developed at the institute. They detected digital traces left by audio production and editing processes that are, at times, inaudible to the human ear.

That included identifying parts of a recording that had been modified or reused, determining whether a recording was an altered version of another file, and assessing whether audio files may have been recorded using the same microphone or recording setup.

Forensic audio researcher Milica Gerhardt observed something unique: that redaction styles varied across the files, along with inconsistencies in how redactions were executed.

"If one observes the content of these audio files, one can see that a lot of personal information has not been redacted," Gerhardt said.

Using the Audio Provenance Suite App, Gerhardt identified two files in the same dataset with identical content, but one was redacted and the other unredacted Image: Stefan Czimmek/DW

In one case, a person called an official tipoff hotline to report information for use in an investigation into Epstein's abuse. In the redacted version, you can hear the person's name, but their phone number was bleeped out.

The same dataset, however, also contained a different version of the audio file, in which the person's full name could be heard as well as their direct contact. Alleged witnesses or informants were apparently not included in the protections allotted to victims.

"They could and should have done a better job on the redactions," said Patrick Aichroth, who heads the MDS group at the Fraunhofer Institute, which has consulted on audio-related evidence for judicial authorities in Germany.

"There is a reason why such material is treated so carefully in court cases," Aichroth said. "Once sensitive or identifying information is disclosed, the damage cannot be undone."

Redactions across audio files were inconsistent and revealed sensitive information, according to audio forensics researchers. Image: Stefan Czimmek/DW

DOJ's redaction failures

DW's investigative unit confronted the DOJ with its findings, including examples in which survivors' personally identifiable information remained in the official Epstein Library.

The DOJ did not respond.

In April, the DOJ's Office of the Inspector General, an independent watchdog tasked with investigating misconduct within the department, announced that it was "initiating an audit of DOJ's compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act."

"Our preliminary objective is to evaluate the DOJ's processes for identifying, redacting and releasing records in its possession as required by the Act," the office said in a statement.

In July, several lawmakers introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which would allow sexual abuse survivors and the governments of US states to take the DOJ to court for failing to comply with the rules laid out in the initial Transparency Act, which had guaranteed that the personally identifiable information of survivors would be protected.

Survivors whose information was published unredacted have since shared accounts of harassment, humiliation and physical threats. With the publicly disclosed information still available on public platforms and, in some cases, still on the DOJ website, the impact continues to upend survivors' lives.

"While the rich and powerful remain protected by redactions, my name was exposed to the world," said the sexual abuse survivor who gave her testimony to Congress in May.

"The evidence is right here," she said, "yet those in power [would] rather us die socially, emotionally and physically than admit their own complicity."

Editor's Note: This article was originally published on July 30, 2026, and updated on July 31, 2026, to clarify that DW observed more than 500,000 fewer files in its February collection of the Epstein Library than were present in an earlier archived version, a discrepancy that may not solely be attributable to file removals.

Edited by: Mathias Bölinger, Milan Gagnon

Technical and data analysis by: Andreas Giefer

Data journalists: Gianna Grün, Rodrigo Menegat Schuinski

Fact checking by: Birgitta Schülke

World.title: Japan: Death toll rises to 34 after deadly earthquake
World.content:
Skip next section 'The strongest quake I have ever experienced'

07/29/2026 July 29, 2026 'The strongest quake I have ever experienced'

Earthquake survivors have been describing the moment the 7.1 magnitude quake struck Japan's southwestern Kumamoto region.

"It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced," 73-year-old businessman Kanzo Matsuomoto told the AFP news agency. "I'm not sure if the region will recover from the damage."

Tokito Kitagawa was riding his motorcycle at the time of the earthquake and said: "Suddenly, there was a huge noise. I couldn't stay on my feet. I had to crouch down."

Kiyoshi Matsunaga, 74, was heading to the supermarket checkout just a few streets away from the collapsed Aeon shopping mall when the shaking began.

"I was frightened," he told the Associated Press, describing items being scattered from the supermarket shelves.

"I thought a bomb had gone off," Takateru Sonoda, 41, who runs a combined hair salon and café near the mall, told local news agency Jiji Press.

"There were people calling on others to evacuate and sirens were ringing out. Nearby roads were gridlocked, it ​was a state of panic."

Yuki Kiyozumi, deputy chief priest at a nearby temple, had just returned home from a meeting and was about to feed her cat. She recalled how she had to crawl on the floor because the shaking was so violent and said: "I don't even know if or how we can rebuild again."

World.title: Giving birth in Serbia: 'You leave your dignity at the door'
World.content:
A months-long DW investigation into childbirth in Serbia revealed a striking pattern in women's negative experiences, the widespread use of practices not universally recommended by the WHO and a system under pressure.

"People say that when you enter Betanija, you leave your dignity at the door. Is that normal?" one woman asked, recalling her experience at the maternity hospital in Novi Sad.

"In my village, they take better care of cows than the doctors took care of me," said another.

"I've never shown anyone my first photo with my baby because in that picture, I look half dead," said a third.

These three women have never met. They gave birth in different Serbian cities, in different years and under the care of different doctors. Yet there is a striking similarity in what they told DW about their experience of giving birth in Serbia.

Over the course of several months, DW spoke with over 20 women in Serbia whose testimonies reveal a similar pattern: inhumane treatment and the routine use of outdated procedures that often serve to compensate for the weaknesses of an overstretched healthcare system rather than respond to the needs of the mother and child.

Birth on the system's terms

In ideal circumstances, childbirth is a physiological process that follows its own rhythm. This is not, however, reflected in practices on many Serbian maternity wards.

In ideal circumstances, childbirth follows its own rhythm. But in Serbia, according to Jasmina Mihnjak, 'women in large maternity wards are treated like they're on an assembly line' Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

Upon admission, women are routinely subjected to the same sequence of procedures: shaving, enemas and a first dose of oxytocin, a hormone used to induce or accelerate labor but one that can significantly increase both pain and the frequency of contractions.

The World Health Organization (WHO) only recommends these practices when there is a clear medical indication or when the woman herself requests them.

"It was so intense and aggressive," recalled Stefani S. from Novi Sad, describing the effects of her first oxytocin stimulation.

"I dilated very quickly, but the pushing contractions never started because they forced me open. Then one doctor after another came to examine me, and eventually one of them ruptured my waters. He didn't say a word. He didn't warn me. He just shoved his hand inside me," she told DW.

"They were forcing a labor that simply hadn't started," said Natasha S. from Ruma, who was also given oxytocin.

When labor continued to progress slowly, doctors resorted to the Kristeller maneuver — the application of manual fundal pressure to the upper part of the abdomen to physically push the baby out. The method is considered controversial by many professional associations because of the risk of injury to both mother and child.

"Afterwards, I had bruises under my breasts. She kept shouting, 'Push!' I was pushing blindly, blood vessels in my eyes burst from pushing the wrong way. Then I heard a doctor say: 'Bring me the vacuum extractor,'" Natasha told DW.

For some mothers who spoke to DW, the joy of welcoming a child into the world was tinged with trauma Image: Cavan Images/IMAGO

Natasha says that her baby developed a swelling on the head after the vacuum extraction. She says she spent the days that followed afraid that there would be more serious complications, including brain hemorrhage and cerebral palsy.

Pressure to speed up labor

The pressure in hospitals to speed up labor often results in another intervention that has become almost routine in Serbia: episiotomy, a surgical incision made in the perineum to facilitate the baby's delivery.

Although the WHO does not recommend the "routine or liberal use of episiotomy" for women undergoing spontaneous vaginal birth, nearly every second woman in Serbia undergoes the procedure. Data collected by DW from maternity hospitals across the country shows that the episiotomy rate in some institutions exceeds 70%.

Episiotomy wounds can make recovery and newborn care more difficult. Many women who spoke to DW said that the procedure was carried out without explanation, without consent and in some cases without anesthesia.

For decades, episiotomies were routinely performed, especially on first-time mothers, because doctors believed they accelerated birth and prevented more severe tearing. Current medical guidelines no longer support such routine use, but old habits apparently die hard.

'Outdated medical assumptions'

Biljana Stankovic, a psychologist who has spent years researching obstetric practices in Serbia, warns that some of these procedures are rooted not only in outdated medical assumptions but also in gender stereotypes.

In her research, she documented testimonies about the so-called "husband stitch" — an extra stitch allegedly used to restore the vagina "to its former size" after childbirth.

"The last time I heard about it was from a woman in Belgrade who said that […] her doctor commented: 'Here's a little bow for the husband,'" Stankovic says.

Verbal abuse

Many of the women interviewed by DW reported being called spoiled, weak, rude, disobedient or even selfish by medical staff during labor.

"At one point I said, 'Please tell me what's happening, it will make it easier.' And they just laughed, like: 'What is she talking about? Nothing will make it easier,'" recalled Stefani. "The man who delivered my baby barely spoke to me at all. He was annoyed because they had woken him up during the night shift."

The 2022 Report on the Treatment of Women in Gynecological and Obstetric Institutions in Serbia shows that the experiences related to DW are not isolated incidents Image: Andrej Isakovic/AFP

That such experiences are not isolated incidents is reflected in the 2022 Report on the Treatment of Women in Gynecological and Obstetric Institutions in Serbia.

Its authors identified verbal abuse as one of the most common forms of mistreatment reported by women during childbirth.

One woman said that midwives threatened to "wake her up with slaps" if she fainted. Others described humiliating and sexualized remarks.

A system under strain

But why does all this happen?

Experts point to a healthcare system under increasing strain.

Data obtained by DW shows that one third of all births in Serbia take place in just four major maternity hospitals in Belgrade and Novi Sad, while smaller facilities across the country continue to close.

"Because of the sheer number of births, women in large maternity wards are treated like they're on an assembly line — everything has to be finished within 24 to 48 hours so the bed can be freed up for the next patient," Jasmina Mihnjak, editor of the parenting platform "Svet za nas" (World for us), told DW.

Not everyone, however, believes that a lack of resources is the only explanation.

Data also shows that two-thirds of maternity wards in Serbia handle no more than three births per day. Under such circumstances, said one gynecologist who wanted to remain anonymous, women could be given more time for labor to progress naturally. Instead, "habit" and "routine" often prevail.

"That's just how it's done," he said.

Will new guidelines bring change?

The new National Guideline for Good Clinical Practice: Physiological Vaginal Birth produced by the Serbian Health Ministry acknowledges many of the problems women have been highlighting for years and recommends different approaches.

Serbia's new National Guideline for Good Clinical Practice: Physiological Vaginal Birth acknowledges many of the problems women have been highlighting for years Image: Andrej Isakovic/AFP

"These testimonies from patients and pregnant women were shocking to us at first. But they also had positive effects on our profession," says Dr. Olivera Kontic, one of the guideline's authors.

Experts warn, however, that Serbia already has numerous guidelines and strategic documents that remain poorly implemented.

"There is no monitoring mechanism to show whether any of these recommendations are actually being applied," says psychologist Biljana Stankovic.

As a result, more women are turning to legal action, says Sanja Radivojevic of the Belgrade Centre for Human Rights. She argues that these cases involve clear violations of patient rights, abuse and infringements of constitutional protections of physical and psychological integrity.

"We had a case where a woman explicitly refused a vacuum extraction and said she understood the risks. They performed it anyway while four or five men held her down," Radivojevic says.

Yet not a single case of what is commonly referred to as obstetric violence has reached a final court judgment in Serbia. Radivojevic fears that if they ever do, prosecutors will side with the system and allow the cases to expire under statutes of limitation.

Meanwhile, many women leave maternity wards carrying more than a baby. For some, the fear and trauma outlast the birth itself.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

The research for this article was conducted with the support of Journalismfund Europe .

World.title: Pakistan: Bodies found after international mountaineers vanish on Broad Peak
World.content:
Rescuers were looking for an international group of climbers, including famous mountaineer Nirmal Purja, following a suspected avalanche at Pakistan's Broad Peak mountain. Authorities say several bodies have been found.

Pakistani rescuers backed by military helicopters found four bodies on Friday after a suspected avalanche on Broad Peak mountain.

The team, which includes renowned Nepal-born British mountaineer Nirmal Purja, lost contact with base camp yesterday, according to the Alpine Club of Pakistan.

What do we know about the missing mountaineers?

Two Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters joined the operation on Friday, while an experienced ground team deployed to the area where the group of at least 10 climbers was last believed to have been.

"The team has been out of communication since Thursday," Alpine Club vice president Karrar Haidri said.

Authorities were in contact with the climbers' families, he added.

Pakistani security sources said the four bodies were located but had not ‌yet ​been recovered.

Chhang Dawa Sherpa, a director at trekking company Seven Summit Treks, said the climbers were believed to have been swept away by an avalanche at around 6,600 meters (21,650 feet).

The Alpine Club said also said it had received "deeply concerning reports" that the avalanche struck the expedition around midday on Thursday.

"The Alpine Club of Pakistan is closely monitoring the situation and coordinating with all concerned stakeholders," the organization said.

One of the missing climbers is Nepal-born Nirmal Purja, who climbed the world's 14 highest peaks in under seven months (file photo) Image: Subash Shrestha/Pacific Press/IMAGO

It added that it remained hopeful the missing climbers would be found safely.

The missing group includes five Nepalese climbers, Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi, an Omani climber identified as Nathira, US climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese climber identified only as Wang and another international climber.

Three Sherpa guides from Seven Summit Treks were among those missing.

Who is Nirmal Purja?

Purja, widely known as Nims Dai, is a former British Army soldier who served with the Brigade of Gurkhas and later became the first Gurkha accepted into Britain's elite Special Boat Service.

He rose to international prominence after climbing all 14 of the world's mountains above 8,000 meters in 189 days in 2019.

The achievement was featured in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing is Impossible."

What is Broad Peak?

Broad Peak stands at just over 8,000 meters in Pakistan's Karakoram range, close to the border with China. It is the world's 12th-highest mountain and lies only a few kilometers from the better-known K2.

Originally designated K3 during the surveying of the Karakoram, its more modern name refers to its unusually wide summit ridge, which stretches for roughly 1.5 kilometers (just under a mile).

The region contains five of the world's 14 peaks above 8,000 meters and attracts climbers from across the globe, although avalanches and rapidly changing weather make expeditions particularly dangerous.
